articles.title: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
articles.body:
In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale.
The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague.
This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it.
“You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement.
“The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that.
“[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there. It could just be a building block, and the US is going to lay out more later with that. To me that would make logical sense, if that was the plan.”
What the plan actually is has never been made clear, and Meink, in his announcement, stressed it was unlikely ever to be.
“Me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else,” he said.
But as Russia and China, both US adversaries, have advanced their own aggressive outer space ambitions and agendas, Trump has responded by placing an ever-increasing focus on militarizing the heavens.
During his first term of office, he created Space Force, the first new, separate branch of the US military in more than seven decades. Last month, he signed an executive order designating the first US Space Academy, a proposed joint civilian-military institution modeled on the army and navy training academies at West Point and Annapolis, to be sited at an as-yet unnamed location.
This week, Military Times reported plans to recruit and train 10,000 new guardians, as Space Force service members are known, to join uniformed ranks within the next five years.
Gen Dan Caine, who as chair of the joint chiefs of staff is the country’s most senior military leader, told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland this week, that the armed forces including Space Force must be “prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”.
Added to a number of other maneuvers and bold pronouncements Trump has made concerning space in recent weeks and months, it is hard not to see the space weapons reveal by Meink – who holds a civilian position reporting to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – as a further blending of the traditionally separate military and non-military roles of US space policy.
In August, the White House unveiled a national space transportation policy that gives Hegseth, as head of the defense department, new responsibility and authority to determine with the chief of Nasa, Jared Isaacman, who manages all US space launches, and sets an ambitious, expansive federal target of more than 1,000 launch and reentry operations by 2030.
The president, meanwhile, has made no secret of his desire for US astronauts to beat China and land on the moon before he leaves office in January 2029; and in March laid out plans, arguably rooted more in optimism than expectation, to invest $20bn (£15bn) on a moonbase to secure for the US the first permanent foothold on the lunar surface.
Some analysts see an almost sea change in the way the Trump administration has approached space in pursuit of its geopolitical goals, compared to previous presidents who upheld decades of separation between the government’s civilian and military needs.
“The way that the US has structured it since Nasa was established in the late 1950s was we have a civil space organization focused on civil exploration, on science, and then we have the Pentagon,” Swope said.
He continued: “There seems to be a tendency to pull them together more than we’ve seen in the past [and] the creation of the Space Academy is just another data point that suggests that at least within the eyes of this administration, the missions are very not just complementary, but very, very similar.
“The civilian space agency and Pentagon, [it’s] not just that they complement each other, but that they’re essentially doing the same mission.”
Certainly, Trump has become more visible in space circles since inviting Isaacman, at the second time of asking, to lead Nasa. Seen as an ally of Elon Musk, the billionaire SpaceX chief and former political acolyte of the president, Isaacman has proven a staunch Trump loyalist in social media posts and in public appearances.
It was the “experience of a lifetime”, Isaacman gushed on X, to accompany Trump on Air Force One to the Johnson Space Center in Houston last month, where the academy announcement was staged before rows of Nasa’s civilian astronaut corps bedecked in their blue flight suits.
In a separate, lengthier post, Isaacman defended the need for a space academy with military theming, arguing that US ambitions necessitated “a bright new generation educated and prepared for this environment”.
He wrote: “If you understand the increasingly important and contested environment above us, then [the academy] is as timely and necessary today as the Space Force has already proven to be.”
The argument that the academy blurs the line between peaceful applications in space and the military, he said, “may be the weakest argument I have seen”, before chronicling a succession of previous Nasa missions and operations that were classified and defense department-based, and noting the agency’s early rockets were modified and evolved from military ballistic missiles.
“Nasa’s mission is as peaceful as it is patriotic,” he said. “We explore for the benefit of all humankind, but we go there under our flag. That mission would be impossible without the Guardians standing watch over the domain as we venture outward.”
Lori Garver, a former deputy administrator of Nasa during the Biden administration, said that while she saw the academy as potentially helpful to the US space program and its future workforce, she was concerned it conflated the agency’s mission for peaceful, civil space exploration with Space Force’s military goals.
“Nasa’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” she told the science publication Ars Technica. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.”
Others say it is difficult, or impossible, for the US to remain committed to the 1967 Outer Space treaty that mandated, among other regulations, that all nations use space for peaceful, non-militarized ends when some countries are blatantly defying it.
US intelligence agencies said in 2024 they were monitoring the development of a new Russian space weapon with the capability of shooting down satellites in Earth’s orbit. Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the Space Force combat forces command, told reporters at the Maryland conference that China was “actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space”, which the country has denied.
A Space Force “threat fact sheet” details how Russia and China are both “testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities with the intent to disrupt and degrade US space-enabled capabilities”.
So, to Swope, the CSIS analyst who worked for the Central Intelligence Agency’s directorate of science and technology for more than a decade, the US’s declaration that it had deployed space weapons of its own was more significant than the absence of detail.
“It’s this idea of space superiority, ‘I want to use space, I don’t want my adversary to’,” he said. “That’s just where we are today.
“Is more of that happening in space? I don’t think this announcement is determining that, or even accelerating that. It may be more just a recognition that the US has woken up to it, and we may just not know it because it’s not public.”
Another question, he said, is what kind of weapons the US may have. “It has talked previously about systems that operate in the electromagnetic spectrum, for jamming or interference with radio signals, that’s what we know publicly about what is in the US counter-space arsenal,” he said.
“War is really bad whether it is confined to Earth or orbit, and maybe we need to have a better thought not just on how we could limit specific types of weapons, but that we want to avoid generally.
“You can’t just walk into a quote-unquote space war and expect that not to be ugly.”

articles.title: US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
The US military's price tag for the Iran war has grown to $43.6 billion as of 3 September, according to a new estimate provided this week to lawmakers.
The figure from US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched by the United States and Israel on 28 February.
A Congressional Budget Office report released Tuesday said the war had cost $38 billion through 1 August and will continue to rack up expenses of around $3 billion a month depending on the conflict's intensity.
The new breakdown, seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Punchbowl News, also showed the continued use of expensive munitions by American forces.
Weapons costs jumped by more than $6 billion in just over a month, from $21.7 billion listed in the CBO report to $28.1 billion in US Central Command’s estimate.
The financial cost is just one measure of the impact of the Iran war, which also is affecting oil prices and the stock market and has led to deaths and injuries of American troops.
The political costs will be calculated in November's midterm congressional elections, with Republicans facing increasing headwinds from the war's unpopularity.
The US military's one-page breakdown to Congress includes costs for operating warships, planes and bases as well as for equipment losses and medical support for troops.
Casualties tallied by the Pentagon have included 18 dead and more than 830 wounded, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System.
The report does not include damage to US bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released Monday said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
In the new report to Congress, the figure for munitions was by far the largest, constituting well over half of all costs. The advanced weapons that have been in the most demand are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems.
The diminished stockpiles also have caused alarm in Europe, where U.S. and NATO officials have told the AP that there is a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors.
Saudi Arabia also is running low on interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for assistance as its standoff with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on.
(The Associated Press)

articles.title: Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
articles.body:
Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
President Vladimir Putin has ordered the Russian subsidiaries of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin placed under temporary management owing to Western support for Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and economic infrastructure.
Moscow introduced the temporary management mechanism in 2023 in response to Western companies leaving Russia and the seizure of Russian state and private assets abroad. Officials said it was intended to keep strategically important businesses operating and shield the economy from decisions by “unfriendly” countries.
On Thursday, Putin amended the 2023 decree to add the Russian assets of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin to the list. All three were transferred to L.E.V. Management, a business and management consultancy.
Why now?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the companies’ home countries and their support for Kiev were major factors behind the decision.
“We are talking about European companies, companies from unfriendly countries,” he told journalists on Friday. “These are unfriendly countries that are actively involved in military actions against our country,” Peskov said, adding that some also support Ukrainian strikes “against our civilian economic infrastructure.”
Why these companies?
Auchan and Leroy Merlin are controlled by France’s Mulliez family through ELO Group and ADEO respectively. Nestle’s Russian business was controlled by subsidiaries of the Swiss food giant.
France has been one of Kiev’s major military backers throughout the conflict. President Emmanuel Macron also pushed a “forward deterrence initiative” earlier this year that could see French nuclear weapons deployed elsewhere in Europe.
Moscow has warned that such a strategy could backfire, saying it cannot “ignore an obvious buildup of the nuclear component of NATO’s joint potential.”
Switzerland, meanwhile, has backed EU sanctions against Russia, prompting Moscow to designate it an “unfriendly nation.” Bern has also considered easing restrictions on the re-export of Swiss-made weapons to Ukraine, sparking criticism from the country’s largest party that its longstanding neutrality is being eroded.
Strikes on Russian infrastructure
The takeover also comes amid continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Ukraine has recently targeted warehouses and logistics facilities belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, and its rival Ozon. Kiev has acknowledged deliberately striking the facilities, claiming their networks are used by the Russian military to procure, store and transport dual-use goods. Moscow rejects the allegations and has denounced the attacks as terrorism.
Ukrainian media reported in July that French intelligence was providing “critical targeting assistance” for strikes on at least eight Wildberries facilities, as well as refineries and other infrastructure.
How important is Russia to the companies?
Russia has been a significant market for the French retailers. At its peak, Auchan Russia was one of the country’s largest foreign retail chains and was still operating around 230 stores as of 2025. ELO reported in 2023 that Russia generated 10% of its revenue, making it the group’s third-largest market after France and Spain.
ADEO relinquished operational control of its Russian subsidiary in 2023, handing management to local executives. However, documents obtained by French investigative outlet L’Informe indicated that ADEO continued to classify the operation as a subsidiary and an “autonomous business unit.”
Leroy Merlin, rebranded as Lemana PRO in Russia in 2024, remained a major source of revenue for ADEO. L’Informe reported that Russia was the group’s second-largest market by revenue after France in 2024 and accounted for around 18.5% of its worldwide revenue in 2025.
Nestle has less exposure. Its Russian operations account for about 1% of global sales, according to Jean-Philippe Bertschy, an analyst at Swiss investment bank Vontobel. RBK estimated Nestle Russia’s revenue at 258 billion rubles ($3.06 billion) in 2025.
How have the companies reacted?
Auchan and Lemana PRO said they had received no official notification from the Russian authorities about the status of their assets and had requested clarification. Both said their stores were operating normally as of Friday.
Nestle said it “takes note” of the presidential decree and is “assessing the situation and its options.” The company said it would take “all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders.”
What happens to the assets?
Under the 2023 framework, foreign owners temporarily lose control of assets placed under management but do not automatically forfeit ownership.
Some assets have been transferred directly to Russian state bodies. In 2023, the Russian operations of Germany’s Uniper and Finland’s Fortum were placed under the Federal Property Management Agency.
In other cases, Moscow has authorized sales. Putin approved the sale of Goldman Sachs’ Russian subsidiary to Balchug Capital in January 2025.
The system also allows assets to be returned. In March 2025, Italian appliance maker Ariston regained control of Ariston Thermo Rus after announcing its return to the Russian market. The subsidiary had been placed under the temporary management of Gazprom Household Systems the previous year.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in 2025 that cases would be assessed individually. Companies that left under government pressure but preserved jobs, contacts and technology, as well as a buy-back option, could be allowed to return, he said.

articles.title: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict
articles.body:
As he stood in Riyadh last September, the world looked like a very different place for Pakistan’s most powerful man, Gen Asim Munir.
The country’s army chief was there to witness the signing of a historic defence pact with Saudi Arabia, which he had personally orchestrated with the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman.
To Munir, it appeared to be a highly strategic win: Riyadh would provide cash-strapped Pakistan with billions of dollars of life-saving investments and loans. In exchange, Pakistan agreed to train up the Saudi military, and Pakistan’s armed forces would defend Saudi Arabia in the unlikely event of an attack on its territory.
Analysts say it was clear that Pakistan presumed US-Iran relations would soon get back on track and the risk of a conflict sweeping across the Middle East and the Gulf was low.
But a very different scenario soon unfolded. By February, the Middle East was on fire after the US and Israel began bombing Iran – and Iran began firing missiles at the Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, in retaliation.
It did not take long for the war to reinflame Saudi’s conflict with the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel group based in Yemen, and for their fragile truce to collapse. Earlier this month the Houthis made unprecedented territorial gains in Yemen and hit Saudi territory with strikes and drones. Saudi Arabia has responded by pounding Yemen with airstrikes. Some believe a return to full-scale war is on the horizon.
The pressure is now mounting on Pakistan, and particularly Munir. In August, the defence pact with Saudi Arabia was extended to include Turkey and renamed the Mecca joint defence agreement. The countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a defence analyst and senior fellow at King’s College London, said: “I don’t think Asim Munir properly calculated the threats the region was facing – and that Pakistan might need to put its troops on the line quite so soon.”
Saudi Arabia has tens of billions of dollars in fighter jets and war machinery, but it does not have any warfare experience to fight the Houthis, who have proved to be tough, resilient fighters. Pakistan’s forces, trained to deal with the constant menace of India, would be highly valuable on the frontline.
Analysts say that if Saudi Arabia decided to activate the Mecca pact to fight the Houthis, Pakistan would have no choice but to send in its troops, including thousands who are already deployed in Saudi Arabia for training. As well as being a defence partner, Pakistan is almost totally economically and geopolitically dependent on Saudi Arabia, which has recently given the country a lifesaving $8bn (£6bn) in funds and investments.
Last week, Pakistani government ministers and senior military figures gave increasingly bullish statements, confirming their “unconditional” commitment to the pact and saying Islamabad would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia.
But privately, officials in Pakistan are deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. The country is already economically crippled, in a de facto war with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and facing an uncontrollable surge in militancy in its border areas.
To many, an activation of the Mecca pact would be perceived as Islamabad taking a clear stance against Iran. Before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Pakistan had good relations with its neighbour – ties that Munir utilised to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in his attempt to secure a lasting ceasefire. But as the war has dragged on, Pakistan has become increasingly infuriated with Iran, while Tehran has little trust left in Islamabad.
As Siddiqa emphasised, Pakistan joining the fight against the Houthis “would come with major repercussions”. After Iran, Pakistan is home to the second-largest population of Shia Muslims, who would probably rise up in protest against any involvement in strikes on the Houthis.
Iran also maintains good relations with the Taliban in Afghanistan, posing the risk of further provoking one of Pakistan’s biggest security threats and driving militancy and security problems along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border to even deadlier levels.
It also risks inflaming the situation in Balochistan, Pakistan’s unstable border region with Iran, which is home to a long-running and uncontrollable insurgency.
Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in Pakistan’s senate, said that only the very few at the top of Pakistan’s military even knew what conditions and agreements had been made in the Mecca pact. With the military as Pakistan’s de facto rulers, the decision to join was not even put before parliament.
“It will be a disaster for the country if Pakistan jumps into war,” said Abbas. “We are already facing two lethal insurgencies; our economy is in a shambles and inflation has rocketed. If we take Saudi Arabia’s side in this conflict, the country will face chaos, instability and religious division.”
So far, no one has been able to pinpoint what the “red line” would be that would force the pact to be activated. Analysts said Pakistan appeared to be banking on Riyadh’s reluctance to enter into open warfare with Iran by escalating its fight with the Houthis. Turkey has also made it clear it does not want to enter the fray.
“Pakistan will do its best not to get involved in any incursion on Yemeni soil,” said Muhammad Amir Rana, the director of the Islamabad-based Pak Institute for Peace Studies.
Speaking privately, one senior official said he did not think the Saudi crown prince “wants to activate the pact now”.
“If the kingdom plans to send its ground forces, Pakistan would support that,” he said. “But I don’t think Saudi Arabia would start a full-fledged war against the Houthis without American approval and Trump has snubbed them. Right now, the US does not want to open up another front; they prefer talking to Houthis.”
He added: “You can’t predict the future though.”

articles.title: US approves possible $2.7 billion sale to support Ukraine's air defense
articles.body:
The U.S. State Department said on Sept. 18 that it had approved a possible $2.7 billion sale of air defense systems and related equipment and services to Ukraine.
The package includes S-300 Clone and GAM-67 missiles, radar systems for countering drones, range-extended laser-guided air defense systems, counter-drone radars, and mobile launcher modification kits, all of which were requested by Kyiv.
The news comes as Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure while continuing large-scale strikes, including with ballistic missiles.
Ukraine will finance the deal through European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing (FMF) funds appropriated under the previous administration.
"This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic progress in Europe," the statement read.
Ukraine faces a critical shortage of Patriot air defense munitions, the only weapons reliably capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
According to recent U.S. congressional records, Washington is poised to approve the transfer of 10 Patriot interceptor missiles from Germany to Ukraine.
Under U.S. President Donald Trump, Washington ended large-scale defense funding and delivery of U.S. military aid to Ukraine, leaving Kyiv to rely on support from other partners to obtain key weapons systems.
Patriot interceptors have been even harder to come by as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has diverted supplies to the Middle East.

articles.title: North Korea reveals new drone production lines
articles.body:
- North Korean state media showed Kim Jong Un touring drone production lines Sept. 16-18, including a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions.
- The drone's launcher system first appeared publicly at an October 2025 military parade, mounted six per truck on four vehicles.
North Korean state media revealed production lines for at least three types of domestically built drones this week, including a one-way attack drone that resembles Israeli-designed loitering munitions, as part of a factory tour by leader Kim Jong Un reported Sept. 19.
The ruling Workers’ Party newspaper Rodong Sinmun said Kim, the party’s general secretary, inspected “important munitions industry enterprises” from Sept. 16 to 18. Photos accompanying the report showed him walking through an assembly hall containing dozens of small flying-wing drones mounted on stands, alongside separate images of him examining what appeared to be missile or drone airframe components with factory officials.
One drone shown is a one-way attack type visually similar to Israel’s Harop family of loitering munitions, weapons built to fly toward a target and detonate on impact rather than return to base. North Korea unveiled a dedicated launch system for this drone at a nighttime military parade on Oct. 10, 2025, marking the Workers’ Party’s 80th anniversary.
That parade featured four 6×6 trucks, each carrying two stacked rows of three launch containers, for an apparent capacity of six drones per vehicle. The parade followed an August 2024 reveal of prototype airframes styled after Israel’s Harop and Switchblade-style “Hero” loitering munitions, neither of which came with published performance figures at the time.
This week’s images of the attack drone during testing were partly obscured, withholding a clear view of some components, though analysts have suggested the design may be related to a rail-launched drone North Korea has separately tested that uses a small rocket booster to get airborne.
Other drones shown on the factory floor were still semi-complete airframes, but their shape already matched North Korea’s larger reconnaissance-strike drones, the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9.
Both first appeared publicly in July 2023 and have undergone repeated flight tests since. The Saetbyol-4 bears a resemblance to the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk surveillance drone, while the Saetbyol-9, with a wingspan of roughly 20 meters (66 feet), resembles the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper and carries hardpoints that suggest it is built to fire guided weapons rather than only observe. North Korean state media has separately called for expanded production across the country’s drone programs, following Kim’s public push earlier this year to accelerate output.
The factory visit came the same week Kim toured facilities producing a mobile rocket launcher that outside analysts have compared to the U.S. Army’s HIMARS system, and the same week North Korea rejected an International Atomic Energy Agency resolution criticizing its nuclear weapons program.
North Korea has not disclosed the factory locations, production quantities for any of the drones shown, or further technical detail on the attack drone beyond what appears in the partly obscured photos.

articles.title: Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections
articles.body:
Germany news: Campaigns wrap up in two state elections
Published September 19, 2026last updated September 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Elections campaigns are closing in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin ahead of elections on Sunday
- The elections are particularly in the spotlight as a gauge of the strength of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which won a recent state election by a landslide
- A port union has warned that seaports are at significant risk of cyberattacks and sabotage
- The famous Oktoberfest opens in the Bavarian capital, Munich
- Annual anti-abortion marches are to take place in Berlin and Cologne, with some Catholic bishops expected to participate
Here is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of September 19-20, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Kremlin envoy offers economic cooperation to AfD
A senior Kremlin envoy has offered Russian help with Germany's energy supply in cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been widely criticized for its perceived links with Moscow.
The remarks by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy for international economic cooperation, come as voters are set to go to the polls in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday, with the AfD locked in a close race with the ruling Social Democrats (SPD).
"Mecklenburg-Vorpommern will thrive again when affordable, reliable Nord Stream gas returns through joint work with AfD," Dmitriev wrote on X, using the German name for the state.
"Lower energy bills, more jobs and higher growth," he continued.
"No more German energy and industrial suicide," he added, responding to response to a post by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel calling for political change in the state.
Moscow has in the past offered to resume supplying Germany with cheap gas through the Nord Stream pipelines in the Baltic Sea if sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine are lifted.
The AfD has argued that cheaper Russian energy would benefit the German economy and has called for Russian gas supplies to Germany to resume.
However, critics say that Germany's previous reliance on Russian gas made it prone to energy blackmail from Moscow, while buying it would also serve to fuel Moscow's war machine.
Sunday's state election will have no direct bearing on the issue, with Russian pipeline gas subject to European Union sanctions.
Only one of the original four Nord Stream pipeline strands remains intact following explosions that damaged Nord Stream 1 and 2 in 2022. The remaining strand is not in use.
Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
Crowds rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened on Saturday.
Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets.
Beer could not be served until the official opening ceremony at midday, when new Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the environmentalist Greens tapped the first keg with the traditional cry of "O'zapft is" — Bavarian dialect for "It is tapped."
"Hop" over to our story for more about the opening of Oktoberfest.
Driver seriously injured in collision with plane at Munich Airport
The driver of a car operated by a cleaning company has suffered serious injuries in a collision with a plane engine at Munich airport overnight and has been flown to hospital by rescue helicopter, police said Saturday.
The car struck both the engine and then a passenger staircase, a police spokeswoman said, saying that the driver might have been affected by a medical problem before the crash.
The accident, which occurred at around 3. a.m. local time (0100 GMT), is being analyzed to determine the exact cause.
There was never any danger to other people, police said, and flight operations were unaffected.
No scheduled flights are permitted at Munich Airport between midnight and 5 a.m.
Germany's Carsten Breuer seeks to chair NATO Military Committee
Germany's highest-ranking soldier, General Carsten Breuer, is standing as candidate for the post of chair of the NATO Military Committee at a vote to take place on Saturday in Copenhagen.
The post is currently held by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone of Italy.
Breuer, 61, will contend against General Marie Annabelle Jennie Carignan, who is currently Chief of the Defence Staff in Canada.
Breuer himself is the current inspector general of the Bundeswehr, or German armed forces.
The winner of the vote would take over leadership of the NATO Military Committee from July 2027.
The head of the committee is seen as the most influential person in NATO alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (Saceur), a position currently held by General Alexus G. Grynkewich of the US Air Force.
High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban
Charlotte Knobloch, the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has reiterated her call for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.
"A lot about the AfD reminds me today about the path the Nazis took to power," the 93-year-old Knobloch told the daily Augsburger Allegemeine.
She said the party "teems with Jew-haters and extremists" — something she said had already existed before, "but once, such parties disappeared from the scene very fast."
This would not be the case with the AfD, she said: "It has broad support in the population, not least with young people."
The party spouts hatred, including "hatred of Jews," she said.
"Unfortunately, no one has managed to clamp down on it so far, so it needs to be banned," she said, even if this is "perhaps difficult legally."
Knobloch called on voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday to "read the newspaper, listen to the radio and watch TV; then you can't help seeing that the AfD is a profoundly anti-democratic party."
She also warned that Jews in Germany were "literally under fire once more," with much reminding here of the 1920s and early 1930s.
"There is hatred of Jews from right, from left and from the Muslim milieu," she said.
Knobloch herself was recently the target of a death threat following the AfD's landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.
Police raid home of aide to AfD top candidate in Berlin
Police this week searched the home of an aide to the top candidate for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) at Sunday's election in Berlin, Kristin Brinker, media reports have said.
Responding to the reports, Berlin prosecutors said the police had been investigating suspected violations of laws governing the use of explosives and weapons.
According to the prosecutors, the police found no evidence to support those suspicions in the September 15 search but did turn up other items of potential criminal interest.
Reports in the Bild and Berliner Zeitung dailies said the investigators had found Nazi relics and drugs in possession of the 48-year-old aide.
In comments to the Bild, Brinker appeared to downplay the significance of the police finds.
"I never had any indication that he was of that bent. He is simply a collector," she said.
Growing sabotage risk at Germany's seaports — association
German ports on the North and Baltic Seas are facing growing risks to their security, a port association has said.
"The threat situation for German seaports has intensified considerably," Florian Keisinger, the managing director of the Association of German Seaport Operators (ZDS), told the Welt newspaper.
Keisinger said that as major hubs, ports were likely targets for cyberattacks, espionage and sabotage.
Norman Zurke, the managing director of the UVHH, an association representing the interests of employers at the port of Hamburg, told the paper that he felt cyberattacks were the main danger.
"However, the entire logistics sector is also already affected by sabotage," he said.
He said that protecting critical infrastructure was a state responsibility and called for more investment by the federal government in protective measures for the port.
Bundeswehr to hold Hamburg drills
From September 24 to 26, the German armed forces, or Bundeswehr, will be holding drills in Hamburg, entitled Red Storm Charlie, as they have in previous years.
Among other things, they will be cooperating with authorities at the port to rehearse responses to possible crisis situations and procedures for transporting troops and materiel to other locations via the sea.
Last year, some German navy corvettes were sabotaged at a Hamburg shipyard. State prosecutors investigated two employees over the incidents but have so far failed to find any culprits.
Oktoberfest set to begin in Munich
The world-famous Oktoberfest will kick off in Munich on Saturday with a traditional ceremony where the city's mayor taps a first barrel of beer — the liquid focus of the event.
New Munich Mayor Dominik Krause of the Green Party will open the 191st edition on the Theresienwiese festival grounds in the center of the Bavarian city at noon (1000 GMT).
Read this DW preview for everything you need to know about Oktoberfest 2026.
Campaigns wrap up ahead of Sunday elections
Parties vying for power in Sunday's elections in two German states are wrapping up their campaigns with several events.
In the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the leftist environmentalistGreen Party are both holding large rallies.
In Berlin, the center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) will also be staging big events.
Other parties concluded their campaigns on Friday.
Many voters undecided
This comes as a large proportion of voters in both states seem unsure about who they will cast their ballot for.
According to the "Politbarometer Extra" survey by public-service broadcaster ZDF, 21% of voters in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and 23% in Berlin remained undecided as of Thursday evening.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a tight contest is expected between the AfD and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), while the Greens are polling around the 5% needed to enter the state parliament at all.
The state is currently governed by a SPD-Left coalition under Premier Manuela Schwesig of the SPD.
In Berlin, surveys show the CDU in a neck-and-neck race with The Left party, while the BSW could fall below the 5% parliamentary threshold.
Berlin's government currently consists of a coalition between the CDU and the SPD under CDU Mayor Kai Wegner.
Merz's future at stake
Results from the elections could have repercussions at federal level, with Merz's political future under debate after his CDU's drubbing at the hands of the AfD in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.
Surveys in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have shown the CDU polling at just 6%.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen! You join our coverage of all things German as attention across the country is focused on two elections on Sunday: in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.
The parties involved in the polls are holding a last day of campaign events, with particularly the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) under scrutiny after its major win in another eastern state, Saxony-Anhalt, two weeks ago.
But events in the far south of Germany will also be in the spotlight on Saturday as the world-famous Oktoberfest in Munich belies its name once more to get underway in September.
And two major so-called "pro-life" demonstrations will be taking place in Berlin and Cologne, with counterprotests also expected.
Read on here to find out more about happenings in Germany this weekend.

articles.title: Mediators push return to MoU, sirens sound over Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Efforts are underway to push a return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding agreed between Iran and the US in June, a spokesman for Iran's Interior Ministry has said.
The spokesman said that “active diplomacy continues with the president’s participation in the Shanghai and BRICS meetings in India and Kyrgyzstan, and through intensive consultations", in a statement carried by Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.
For his part, US President Donald Trump has said that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons will come with some cost, however predicted that the war would soon end, followed by a drop in fuel prices.
Elsewhere, Saudi Arabia on Friday and early Saturday warned of a “hostile aerial threat” and issued a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom, as fighting with Yemen's Houthi rebels escalates.
Turkey has revoked the licence of Iran's Bank Mellat, a semi-private financial entity that has been subject to Western sanctions for years, the official gazette said early on Saturday.
The decision was announced some two weeks after Washington slapped sanctions on a Turkish bank over alleged ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) although it was not immediately clear whether the two issues were related.
Iran's judiciary announced on Saturday the execution of a man accused of providing information about Iranian missile sites to Israeli intelligence.
"The death penalty was carried out against Hossein Pedaran, who had provided the Mossad with information on missile sites in Isfahan province" in central Iran, judicial authorities said, without saying when he was arrested or put on trial.
Pedaran had faced accusations of "espionage and intelligence collaboration" in favour of Israel.
Saudi sounds first sirens since renewed fighting in Yemen
Saudi Arabia warned of a “hostile aerial threat” after issuing a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom late Friday and early Saturday, and at least one explosion was heard in the capital, Riyadh.
The alert heard in Riyadh was first for the Saudi capital since the latest escalation with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

articles.title: Flawed AI-linked intel almost led US to board China ship: Report
articles.body:
Flawed AI-linked intel almost led US to board China ship: Report
WASHINGTON - The US military came close to boarding a Chinese vessel in the Middle East earlier in 2026 based on a flawed intelligence report prepared with the help of artificial intelligence, CNN said on Sept 18.
US intelligence indicated the ship was carrying nuclear weapons-related components, leading American forces to prepare to intercept it, the broadcaster reported, citing four anonymous sources familiar with the incident.
But the operation was called off after officials determined that an AI chatbot used by an analyst had misidentified the material the ship was carrying.
CNN quoted one source as saying the intelligence report was “entirely false” but “almost started a war.”
It did not specify what the vessel was actually carrying or where it was bound.
US Central Command – which is responsible for American forces in the Middle East – did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reported incident.
The CNN report comes after a furore erupted earlier in September when a researcher publicly resigned from leading AI firm Anthropic over fears that the technology could escape human control.
Another Anthropic employee, who did not resign, stated publicly that “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and that he thought the chances were greater than “10 per cent within the next decade.”
Despite the warnings, US President Donald Trump and some of his key allies have voiced opposition to drastically curbing the development of artificial intelligence.
In a separate incident involving the US military and China, Politico reported on Sept 18 that F-35 jet parts – including a sensitive stealth canopy for a cockpit – were diverted to Hong Kong and are now missing, raising fears that Beijing had obtained sensitive American military technology.
The parts were headed from Australia to the United States for repairs when the diversion occurred, the US outlet reported, adding that it was unclear why the parts were rerouted or where they are now.
A spokesperson for Lockheed Martin, which manages the F-35 supply chain, said the company could not discuss specific shipments because of “security reasons”.
“Lockheed Martin follows all US regulations established by the Department of War and regulated by the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) regarding the shipment of aircraft components,” the spokesperson said.
“Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 programme and the security of our allied partners.” AFP

articles.title: Ukraine Deploys New Interceptor Drone Against Jet-Powered Shaheds
articles.body:
Ukraine has deployed a newly developed interceptor drone to counter Russian jet-powered Shahed strike drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Sept. 19, following an operational briefing from acting Head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) Oleksandr Poklad.
Writing on Telegram, Zelensky stated that the SBU’s military counterintelligence department achieved tangible operational results in intercepting high-speed Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A report from SBU head Oleksandr Poklad. There is a good result from the Security Service’s military counterintelligence in countering jet ‘Shaheds,’” Zelensky stated. “A new interceptor drone has been created and already successfully applied. Step by step, we are moving forward to give Ukraine greater protection.”
Zelensky commended Ukrainian engineers and defense enterprises working to expand production, expressing gratitude to “all developers and manufacturers who work every day to scale the necessary weapons.
Frontline trials and counter-drone scaling
The operational deployment comes as the Ukrainian military accelerates trials of domestic unmanned systems engineered specifically to defeat high-velocity aerial targets.
The Armed Forces of Ukraine are currently evaluating four advanced models of interceptor drones in active combat sectors along the front line to neutralize Russian turbojet-powered strike drones.
UK Military Sites Targeted by Drones Over 300 Times in Year
In addition, approximately 10 other domestic manufacturers are conducting flight and intercept tests of prototype systems before submitting them for formal military codification.
Ukrainian defense planners have prioritized interceptor drones as a cost-effective countermeasure to relieve pressure on ground-based air defenses.
In recent months, Russian forces have escalated launches of jet-powered Geran-4 and Banderol loitering munitions, which travel at speeds between 400 and 600 kilometers per hour at altitudes of several kilometers, rendering conventional mobile anti-aircraft gun teams and propeller-driven interceptors less effective.
Surge in civilian casualties from long-range strikes
The development of domestic interceptors follows a sharp rise in casualties caused by Russian aerial bombardments targeting Ukrainian urban centers away from active combat lines.
August was one of the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine, with at least 372 non-combatants killed and 2,349 injured. The monthly casualty count marked a slight decline from July – which recorded the highest civilian toll of the war – but reflected a 55 percent surge compared to the corresponding timeframe in 2025 and more than double the casualty rate documented in 2024.
According to the UN assessment, long-range weapons served as the primary cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of all deaths and injuries in August, with 194 killed and 1,077 wounded. The majority of these casualties occurred in urban centers far removed from active frontlines, with the highest tolls recorded in Kyiv, Kherson, Kryvyi Rih, and Zaporizhzhia.
Concurrently, short-range tactical drones, particularly first-person view (FPV) loitering munitions, accounted for 30 percent of total civilian casualties nationwide in August, remaining the leading cause of death and injury in frontline communities such as Kherson.
