Shame on the Washington Post — they’re worse than Iranian state media. https://t.co/vU9OkSOnLB
An increasingly unpopular war
Despite US President Donald Trump insisting the war has been a success – even claiming at times that “Americans aren’t against the war” – polling indicates growing public opposition. A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 28% support Trump’s approach to Iran, while 62% disapprove.
The war has also deepened divisions in Congress ahead of the November midterms. Congressional Democrats have overwhelmingly opposed the conflict, making its multibillion-dollar cost and economic fallout – including gasoline prices approaching $5 a gallon – campaign issues. They have also pledged to investigate the Pentagon’s handling of casualty notifications if they retake the majority.
While most House Republicans have voted to block anti-war resolutions, some GOP lawmakers have broken ranks, backing bipartisan efforts to invoke war-powers restrictions or halt funding for the conflict. Representative Thomas Massie (KY) also moved this week to force a House vote on impeaching Hegseth, alleging he violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973 by pursuing hostilities without congressional authorization.
The war has cost the US $43.6 billion through September 3, including $28.1 billion in munitions expended, according to CENTCOM figures shared with lawmakers and the media on Friday. The total excludes extensive damage to US bases across eight Middle Eastern countries. Senior military officials reportedly warned Hegseth last month that prolonged large-scale operations against Iran were unsustainable.
Trump, however, insists the war will end soon, telling reporters last week it would likely stop immediately after the midterms. He told Axios on Thursday that he faces “a big decision” over whether to restart major combat operations to end the conflict.
Iran, meanwhile, has refused to cave to Trump’s threats, with Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warning earlier this month of “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation against further US aggression. On Friday, Tehran showcased a new volunteer force that will receive limited military and emergency training to support the IRGC. IRGC chief Hassan Hassanzadeh told state broadcaster IRIB that over 600,000 people had registered, with more than one million expected to undergo training.

articles.title: India’s homegrown air defense system finds new buyers
articles.body:
- Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash air defense missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
- Armenia remains the only other confirmed foreign Akash buyer, having signed for the Mk 1S variant with deliveries starting in late 2024.
Former DRDO Chairman Samir Kamat said India has exported its Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, extending New Delhi’s defense export reach into Central Asia for the first time.
The Akash is a medium-range air defense system built to intercept aircraft, helicopters, drones and cruise missiles. Bharat Dynamics Limited manufactures the missile, using radar and command-and-control systems developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation. Kamat did not specify how many systems were delivered, their configuration, or the value of the deals.
His statement follows earlier reporting in August that said Turkmenistan and Tajikistan were negotiating purchases of the newer Akash Mk 1S variant but had not yet signed formal contracts. It is not clear whether the exports Kamat described represent those same deals reaching completion, or a separate delivery. Neither Indian officials nor the two Central Asian governments have released further detail.
Armenia was the first, and until now the only confirmed, foreign buyer of the Akash system, signing a deal for the Mk 1S variant and beginning deliveries in late 2024. That sale gave India a track record it has pointed to since in pitching the system elsewhere in the former Soviet space.
The Mk 1S upgrade adds an Indian-developed active radio-frequency seeker for terminal homing, on top of the command guidance the missile uses during its mid-course flight. That combination is meant to improve accuracy against maneuvering targets and make the missile harder to defeat with electronic jamming than the original, purely command-guided Akash. The system uses India’s Rajendra phased-array radar to track and engage multiple targets at once, a capability suited to defending fixed sites and stretches of border rather than a single point target.
Tajikistan and Turkmenistan currently rely mainly on older Soviet and Russian-made air defense equipment, including S-125, Kub, Buk and S-300 systems. Aging stockpiles and changing aerial threats have pushed both countries to look at diversifying their suppliers, a dynamic Armenia’s earlier purchase is seen as having encouraged elsewhere in the region. As with Armenia, where the initial missile sale was followed by additional purchases of Indian radar, artillery, rocket systems and vehicles, further Indian defense sales to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan could follow if the Akash purchases are confirmed.
The moves would add to a broader shift in Central Asia’s arms market, a region long dominated by Russian suppliers, toward a wider set of options that now includes India’s defense industry.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Command Posts and Training Ground
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck multiple Russian drone command posts, a military training ground, logistics facilities, and an ammunition depot across occupied areas of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions on Friday, Sept. 18, and Saturday, Sept. 19, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
According to the military update published on Facebook, Ukrainian forces conducted targeted strikes against unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command posts in both active combat sectors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the Zaporizhzhia region, precision strikes engaged drone command centers near Volodymyrivka, Verbove, Dobropillya, and Rivnopillya, alongside two distinct UAV control posts located in the vicinity of Novoprokopivka.
Ukrainian units also targeted the Russian military’s “Vostochny” training ground situated near the occupied settlement of Novopetrivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Donetsk region, strikes hit Russian UAV command posts in the areas of Luhanske and Pokrovsk. Ukrainian forces additionally engaged logistical infrastructure, striking a material and technical supply warehouse in Rybynske and an ammunition storage depot near Amvrosiivka.
The General Staff also confirmed battle damage assessments from prior cross-border operations, verifying that a Ukrainian strike on Sept. 17 damaged a Russian 80P6 radar station deployed near the settlement of Mityuli in Russia’s Smolensk region.
UK Military Sites Targeted by Drones Over 300 Times in Year
Airfield and refinery strikes in Rostov and Yaroslavl
The strikes against Russian tactical command and rear storage assets follow a series of coordinated long-range drone operations conducted on Sept. 17 targeting strategic installations inside Russia.
In that overnight operation, long-range attack drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine’s (SBU) “Alpha” Special Operations Center struck the Rostov-Tsentralny military airfield in Rostov-on-Don.
SBU assessments confirmed direct hits on six aircraft in the airfield’s parking sector: one An-12 military transport plane, two An-26 transport aircraft, and three helicopters, triggering fires and secondary detonations. Regional authorities reported that falling debris also damaged an electrical transformer substation, cutting power across four municipal districts.
Concurrently, a joint operation by the SBU, the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR), and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) damaged the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery in Yaroslavl, located roughly 250 kilometers northeast of Moscow.
The facility ranks among Russia’s five largest oil refineries, with an annual processing capacity of approximately 15 million metric tons. Drone impacts ignited structural fires at the plant and prompted the temporary closure of a section of the M-8 highway connecting Yaroslavl with the Russian capital.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the engagements in Rostov and Yaroslavl, characterizing the precision operations as part of a systematic asymmetric response designed to degrade Russian air power, military logistics, and wartime industrial capacity.

articles.title: Germany Must Prepare Entire Society for War, Military Chief Warns
articles.body:
Germany must mobilize its entire society, commercial industry, and armed forces to prepare for national defense and the potential risk of war, Inspector General of the Bundeswehr Carsten Breuer warned, Bild reported.
Speaking at the IISS Prague Defense Summit, Germany’s highest-ranking military officer emphasized that military hardware and cutting-edge technology alone cannot safeguard the country against evolving security challenges.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Breuer observed that rapid technological acceleration causes frontline tactics to become obsolete quickly, stressing that German defense planners must systematically analyze the operational lessons emerging from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Russia learns. They copy and adapt, introducing innovations aimed at our strengths and bypassing them. Technology should not determine what we do. We must determine what we do with technology,” Breuer stated.
He stressed that resisting hybrid operations and modern warfare demands a comprehensive, resilient posture that extends far beyond the organic capabilities of the armed forces.
Addressing the German public directly, Breuer underscored the vital role of civilian commitment in national deterrence.
“Without you, we soldiers are doomed to fail. But failure is not an option. Because that would mean a fatal threat to our societies as we know them. We are all in the same boat,” the general said.
South Korea Signs Pact With EU on Satellite Network
2029 operational readiness mandate
Breuer’s warning aligns with his standing strategic directive ordering the Bundeswehr to achieve full operational combat readiness by 2029 to deter potential Russian aggression against NATO territory.
The readiness target is supported by legislative adjustments easing Germany’s constitutional debt brake for defense appropriations, allowing Berlin to inject substantial long-term capital into modernizing the military.
The procurement framework prioritizes expanding multi-layered integrated air defenses, procuring long-range precision strike systems, scaling electronic warfare capabilities, and replenishing critical ammunition stockpiles.
The strategic timeline reflects intelligence assessments shared across NATO suggesting that Moscow could reconstitute its conventional military forces, scale domestic industrial output, and position itself to challenge allied frontiers within five years.
Leipzig airport sabotage and Russian hybrid threats
The military leadership’s urgent appeal arrives amid acute vigilance across Germany following a thwarted Russian-directed sabotage operation at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4.
During that incident, an attempted drone strike targeting a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft failed only because a detonator wire broke, leaving approximately 1.8 kilograms of Semtex explosive concealed inside a vegetable tin can unexploded.
German investigators determined that a detonation would have caused structural damage to the logistics hub, as the cargo aircraft held roughly 25,000 liters of aviation fuel at the time of the attempt.
German security services identified two primary operatives linked to the plot: Belarusian national Andrei K. and Russian national Oleg L., assessing that the operation was coordinated on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence directorate (GRU). Polish prosecutors separately linked Andrei K. to a major state-sponsored arson attack against a commercial center in Łódź in 2024.
Forensic tracking showed that the explosives were smuggled into Germany through Balkan freight routes and cached near the airfield.
In response to the plot, the German government publicly attributed the sabotage to Russian intelligence agencies on Sept. 1 and ordered the expulsion of approximately 60 Russian diplomats alongside the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn by Sept. 18, underscoring the growing convergence of asymmetric sabotage and conventional deterrence facing German defense planners.

articles.title: Democratic Leaders Fear the New Russia Sanctions Bill Could 'Harm' Americans. Here's Why
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Friday signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine.
The legislation, which also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors, has been hailed for its harsher measures on Russia, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling it “an extremely powerful tool.” However, Democratic leaders have expressed grave concern over the broader tariff authority it affords to Trump.
The new law allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that make “new purchases of crude oil or natural gas” originating from Russia, or any country among the top five importers of Russian oil or gas over the last 12 months.
According to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), the top three purchasers of Russian oil and gas in August were China, India, and Turkey.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, says Trump’s previous ambition to introduce tariffs using any available avenue has ignited the concern among Democrats.
“The reason why people are so nervous about this is that the authority is extremely wide, and has been handed to an Administration that has already shown great latitude to follow the spirit of the law,” Elms tells TIME. “Tariffs could be set at 100%. It's really at the discretion of the Executive Branch.”
Democratic leaders sound the alarm on “terribly flawed” bill
The House passed the bill with bipartisan support on Wednesday. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named in honor of the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure, passed with 262 votes to 159. Some 58 Democrats voted with the majority of Republicans in favor of the bill, despite objections from party leadership.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries led the Democratic opposition to the bill, raising concerns over extending Trump new tariff powers that he said could "give the President an additional tool to visit economic harm on the American people."
“Why in the world would this Congress or the People's House give this President unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” the New York Representative questioned ahead of the vote.
After the bill passed, Jeffries told TIME that Trump “cannot be entrusted with new powers to impose tariffs that will further raise costs for American families.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Shortly after his return to office, Trump implemented global tariffs as part of what he called a “Liberation Day.” Although the majority of those were shut down by a Supreme Court ruling in February that deemed them illegal, his general use—and threatened use—of tariffs has continued to fuel international tensions.
Tariffs introduced since Trump’s return have already made their mark on American households, experts say. The Yale Budget Lab in late August estimated that household costs due to tariffs “total about $1,100 annually under current law.”
The U.S.-Canada has raised fresh concerns over the financial impact on American consumers.
Many Americans are already struggling with the cost of living crisis. The Urban Institute in April found that “49% of people in American families don’t have the resources to cover essential expenses to live securely in their community.”
Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, has also raised concerns about the potential impact on American families.
In the weeks leading up to the Russia sanctions bill, he urged lawmakers to find a “compromise that properly punishes Russia for its illegal war of aggression against the Ukrainian people, while protecting the American people from reckless inflationary tariffs.”
In a statement to TIME after the vote, Meeks said he found it "regrettable" that lawmakers chose not to “place more guardrails” on the bill’s tariff authorities.
Similar concerns were raised by Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, who described the bill as “well intentioned, but terribly flawed” in its efforts to hinder Russia’s war effort against Ukraine. “Trump has abused every tariff authority Congress has delegated to the President,” Beyer told TIME, accusing his colleagues of choosing to “ignore our warnings that he is highly likely to continue that pattern with this bill.”
Beyer had delivered a stark warning on the floor ahead of the vote, insisting the bill “would do more harm than good for America and for Ukraine.”
“Trump has abused every presidential tariff authority—every single one—that Congress has given, often to target our allies. This bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions,” he argued. “He could then hit them with tariffs of up to 100%, with no guardrails or oversight, and no expiration. It’s a much stronger tariff power than those he has already abused, and it would be much harder to challenge in court. Giving him this power when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it would be an incredible mistake.”
Why other Democratic lawmakers supported the legislation
The legislation’s capacity to economically isolate Russia earned it the bipartisan support needed to get the bill to Trump’s desk.
The bill allows for the further introduction of sanctions on persons and financial institutions affiliated with the Russian government, the prohibiting of energy exports and investment into Russia, and blocks the transfer of funds to the Kremlin.
The bill also includes the potential to expand sanctions on Iran, and comes amid growing concerns from the U.S. over the relationship between Moscow and Tehran. The U.S. Treasury on Monday announced the latest sanctions targeting the Russian bank VTB over allegations it is involved “in Iranian sanctions evasion.”
Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, who co-chairs and co-founded the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, is in firm favor of the legislation. ”We're going to pay close attention to the Administration and to see what they're going to do with these new powers that have been given,” she told TIME after the vote.
Kaptur previously said that both the sanctions and tariff measures were “the best chance we have to get bipartisan legislation signed into law to hold Russia accountable and achieve peace.”
Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland also praised the legislation, championing it as an additional way to showcase support for Kyiv. “Today we took a step to redeem our pledge to Ukraine, to support their sovereignty and their democracy,” said Hoyer outside the Capitol. “We will sanction, actively and effectively, Russian criminal behavior.”
How China and India could be impacted by the Russia sanctions bill
The legislation extends Trump the authority to impose tariffs on new and prominent importers of Russian oil and gas.
The legislation could prompt a new wave of tariffs handed out by the President, experts warn. "The tariffs can be introduced across the board," says Elms. “This is what makes it so alarming.”
China and India are two major importers of Russian oil and gas and therefore stand to be the most affected. In August, China was importing roughly 1.25 million barrels of Russian Crude oil daily, according to commodity analysts Kpler via Reuters. India imported record-highs of 2.5 million barrels daily of Russian Crude in June, per Kpler's analysis.
According to The European External Action Service (EEAS), Russia’s shadow fleet—largely unregulated oil tankers transiting sanctioned oil—includes between 600 to 1,400 vessels. Exports are crucial for China and India, the leading importers of seaborne oil from Russia.
U.S. sanctions have already targeted Russian oil tankers and Moscow’s energy industry in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Still, China and India have remained steady buyers, but the threat of tariffs could change the attitude of both countries, experts predict.
“I think they will be quite concerned on this one,” says Elms. “Presumably because of this [bill], we will see some diversification away from Russian energy by India and China.”
While the Supreme Court ruling barring most of Trump’s prior tariffs cited Congressional power to impose tariffs, this argument won’t be applicable if lawmakers attempt to restrict the President’s ability. “In this case, Congress has quite clearly given that authority to the President,” says Elms.
Beijing has hit back firmly against the tariff measures included in the bill. “China opposes long-arm jurisdiction and unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
The legislation comes at a crucial time for U.S.-China relations, just a week ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is also set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, Vice Premier He Lifeng, this weekend.
The U.S. already has a number of tariffs in place on Chinese goods, including a tariff of up to 12.5% on goods allegedly made with forced labor. The U.S. Trade Representative's last year launched a tariff investigation into China's "apparent failure" to comply with the "Phase One" trade deal signed with Trump in 2020.
Meanwhile, India’s Foreign Ministry responded to the new sanctions bill by saying it was “monitoring further developments." The statement said India "remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people" and "will continue to do so through diversified sourcing."
The statement said imports of Russian energy had been discussed with U.S. officials in recent months, and that “implications for not just the bilateral relationship, but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.”
Trump threatened tariffs on Indian goods last August in response to Delhi’s continued purchasing of Russian oil. “They don’t care how many people in Ukraine are being killed by the Russian war machine,” claimed Trump, days ahead of his meeting with President Vladimir Putin that yielded no concrete results.
Similar to China, India also currently faces a tariff on alleged forced labor goods, with the levy landing at 10%.
After agreeing on a framework for a bilateral trade agreement in February, Delhi and Washington have continued negotiations since.
“India and the U.S. have been supposedly a ‘moment away’ from a bilateral agreement,” says Elms. “I think it is highly unlikely now that India will actually sign that agreement because they are now potentially subject to new tariffs at any time.”

articles.title: US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
articles.body:
CHINA CAPITAL
US prosecutors accuse Huawei of ‘far-reaching criminal scheme’ spanning decades
The Chinese tech giant is on trial in New York for allegedly violating U.S. sanctions on Iran and stealing trade secrets as it built its global telecommunications empire.
The U.S. government has long warned, in sweeping terms, that the Chinese tech giant Huawei is effectively an arm of the Chinese state that acts with impunity on the global stage, including allegedly violating U.S. sanctions. Over the last two weeks, U.S. prosecutors have begun to make that case, labeling Huawei a “criminal enterprise,” in what could be a lengthy trial in a New York federal court.
Huawei enacted “a far-reaching criminal scheme extending over twenty years,” according to Department of Justice prosecutor Taylor Stout. “Crime was an important business strategy.”
Nearly eight years after the U.S. Department of Justice unsealed its indictment against Huawei, the company is facing 12 felony charges, including that it conspired to steal technologies from U.S. competitors and business partners. The federal government also alleges that Huawei lied to its Western banking partners about doing business in Iran in violation of U.S. sanctions. No individuals have been charged.
Huawei’s lawyers rejected the government’s characterization, with Brian Heberlig, one of at least a dozen attorneys working for the defense, arguing that the charges concerned “disconnected incidents.”
“It’s about competition, not conspiracy,” Heberlig said.
In December 2018, Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in Vancouver at the request of U.S. officials and charged with fraud. After a lengthy period of house arrest, Meng reached a deferred prosecution agreement with U.S. authorities in 2021 in which she admitted to lying to HSBC and other banks about a Huawei subsidiary’s business in Iran. That admission will likely be introduced during the trial.
As reported in China Capital, ICIJ’s recent investigation into Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Huawei had leaned on its close relations with the state-owned bank to insulate itself from the fallout of Meng’s arrest. After the Justice Department unveiled its indictment, the company’s bankers at ICBC’s London branch facilitated a transfer of $1.3 billion in “emergency cash” from London to a branch in China without informing compliance staff.
The federal government’s investigations of Huawei go back to at least the Obama administration. Some of the alleged crimes occurred around the turn of the century. The allegations include that Huawei stole technology from U.S. companies like the cell service provider T-Mobile and the networking giant Cisco. Prosecutors have claimed that Huawei paid bounties to employees for recruiting workers to leave rivals, bringing their trade secrets to Huawei, which employs about 210,000 people in more than 170 countries and regions. In one incident raised at trial, a Huawei employee allegedly snuck into a booth at a trade show to take photos of Fujitsu network equipment and was spotted by a security guard.
For years, U.S. intelligence and government officials have expressed concern that, along with being a dominant player in global telecommunications, Huawei is a tool of Chinese statecraft, enabling espionage and repression in autocratic countries like North Korea. Huawei’s global expansion, officials warned, might allow the Chinese government to eavesdrop on numerous countries.
In the first days of the current trial, Parham Baheshti, a former engineer at Mobinet, an Iranian telecommunications firm, testified that Huawei, working with Iranian intelligence, built a domestic surveillance system that could spy on users of Mobinet’s wireless network. “They help a dictatorship to rule and suppress people,” Baheshti said.
Huawei’s defense lawyers argued that the company furnished a so-called lawful interception program similar to the ones found in many other countries, both democratic and otherwise, which sometimes run on equipment from Western tech companies.
Judge Ann Donnelly told jurors last week China and the Chinese Communist Party “are not on trial.” But the backdrop of great power competition, especially in a trial that began with a focus on Huawei’s business in Iran in alleged violation of U.S. sanctions, is hard to ignore. Jurors were asked if they had any family ties to China and scrutinized for their opinions on the tech industry.
The trial is one of the biggest in the history of the Eastern District of New York, with hundreds of pieces of evidence expected to be introduced, along with numerous witnesses who have worked for or with Huawei in the U.S., Iran, and other countries. Judge Donnelly said she hopes that proceedings will conclude by Christmas, but the trial may run into next year.
“What is so remarkable is that the case is going to trial,” Duke University Law Professor Brandon Garrett said in an email to ICIJ. “The vast bulk of criminal cases, including corporate cases, are resolved through negotiated settlements. Here, the company has already been sanctioned and may have had little incentive to settle.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet with President Donald Trump on Sept. 24 in Washington, D.C., where they will discuss issues such as AI safety and American citizens imprisoned in China. President Xi has championed Huawei, which just last month reached a potential agreement with the Egyptian government to build AI data centers. The State Department, hoping to stymie a potential victory for China’s tech industry, has reportedly encouraged U.S. companies to outbid Huawei’s offer.
If the world’s largest telecoms firm is eventually found guilty, it’s not clear what the Justice Department, or the Trump administration, may want as restitution.
“Should the government prevail, what consequences can be imposed on top of existing sanctions?” Garrett, the law professor, said. “What assets are available to pay fines, for example, if the company is found liable?”

articles.title: The US nearly started a war with China over an erroneous AI-generated report – CNN
articles.body:
The US nearly started a war with China over an erroneous AI-generated report – CNN
Kyiv • UNN
The US prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on a false report about a nuclear cargo. The AI error was discovered before the operation began.
In the spring, U.S. military personnel prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel based on an intelligence report claiming that the ship was carrying components for a nuclear program. Shortly before the operation began, it was discovered that the analyst had prepared the document using artificial intelligence, which had misidentified the cargo, CNN reports, citing sources, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred in the spring amid the war with Iran. An intelligence report circulated among U.S. military personnel contained information about a Chinese vessel in the Middle East that was allegedly carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons program.
The information was taken so seriously that the U.S. military began planning to intercept the ship. According to CNN sources, armed U.S. service members were preparing to board it, while military aircraft were already in the air.
The error was discovered before the operation began
Only shortly before the planned interception did officials decide to examine in greater detail the report prepared by an analyst from the U.S. Special Operations Command.
It then emerged that artificial intelligence had been used in preparing the document, and that the chatbot had incorrectly identified the materials being carried by the Chinese vessel. CNN was unable to establish what was actually on board.
According to one of the network's sources, the report about the cargo was "completely false."
This nearly started a war
The U.S. military operation against the Chinese vessel could have caused a serious escalation in relations between Washington and Beijing and potentially developed into an armed confrontation between the two countries.

articles.title: Putin Accuses Ukraine of Sabotaging Peace Negotiations
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Ukraine is unwilling to engage in genuine peace negotiations, asserting that Kyiv is actively taking steps to prevent a diplomatic resolution to the war.
Addressing a meeting of Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Friday, Sept. 18, Putin alleged that Ukrainian calls for diplomatic engagement are disingenuous, state news agency Interfax reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin claimed.
The Russian leader contended that Moscow cannot be intimidated and insisted that recent Ukrainian actions demonstrate a refusal to negotiate. His remarks follow a series of Ukrainian drone strikes on defense-industrial and refining facilities across western and central Russia, as well as recurring cross-border engagements.
Despite the Kremlin’s accusations, Ukrainian officials have repeatedly presented diplomatic initiatives to end hostilities, including proposals for an unconditional ceasefire and direct leader-level talks.
However, Moscow has consistently conditioned any diplomatic engagement on sweeping political concessions, including international recognition of its illegal annexations and Kyiv ceding control of remaining areas in the Donbas.
US Approves $2.68B Air Defense Equipment Sale to Ukraine
Putin’s true goal
Putin’s assertions contrast with assessments delivered earlier in the week by President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned that the Kremlin leader remains fundamentally committed to destroying Ukrainian sovereignty rather than settling a localized territorial dispute.
Zelensky stated that Putin’s ambition extends far beyond consolidating occupied frontline territory.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said, responding to US mediation concepts focused on drawing new territorial borders. “He needs Ukraine. He needs Ukraine to be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remains prepared for an unconditional cessation of hostilities if Moscow halts combat operations along the existing line of contact, allowing international mediators to facilitate diplomatic talks.
However, he firmly dismissed the concept of a “win-win” compromise promoted by external mediators, arguing that an unprovoked war that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives cannot yield mutual benefit.
The president reaffirmed his readiness to meet Putin directly if such an encounter could produce concrete progress toward a lasting peace, while reiterating that robust Western security guarantees remain essential to prevent Russia from using an operational pause to prepare future offensives.
Washington weighs pre-settlement economic incentives
The diplomatic impasse arrives amid reports that the administration of US President Donald Trump is exploring preliminary commercial agreements with Moscow before achieving a definitive peace settlement.
Washington is assessing whether concluding bilateral economic deals could signal seriousness regarding a long-term diplomatic reset and incentivize Russian elites to support ending the war. A US official told the newspaper that business agreements could help persuade hardline figures surrounding Putin that Washington seeks a constructive bilateral framework.
The prospective approach would mark a shift from previous US policy, which insisted that commercial ties and economic normalization could occur only after Russia ends its military aggression against Ukraine. Potential areas of cooperation previously raised by Moscow and Washington have encompassed energy partnerships, critical mineral investments, Arctic transit routes, and corporate joint ventures.
During early September discussions in Moscow between Putin and US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed that talks addressed potential large-scale, mutually beneficial commercial projects alongside conflict settlement concepts.

articles.title: U.S. approves Ukraine air defense package with unclear weapons
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion air defense sale to Ukraine on Sept. 18, funded through European contributions and prior U.S. military financing.
- The package lists "S-300 Clone" and "GAM-67" missiles, designations that don't match any publicly known current weapon system.
The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine on Sept. 18, a package built around several weapons whose exact identity the notification itself does not make clear.
The Defense Security Cooperation Agency’s notification to Congress describes the deal as an “Air Defense Development Upgrade.” Ukraine would pay for it through a mix of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing that Congress appropriated under the prior administration, with that American funding counted as a one-to-one capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund. The sale still needs to clear the standard congressional review period before any contract can be finalized, and the eventual contractors would be chosen through a competitive U.S. government procurement process.
The equipment list includes items called S-300 Clone missiles and GAM-67 missiles, along with Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, a launcher platform called the Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5, mobile launcher modification kits, and RPS 202 counter-drone radars, plus the usual mix of spare parts, software, training publications and logistics support that accompanies most Foreign Military Sales packages.
Two of those names don’t match any publicly known current weapon system. GAM-67 is the U.S. Air Force’s old designation for the Crossbow, a turbojet-powered anti-radar missile program that Northrop’s Ventura Division built in the 1950s. Only 14 were ever produced, and the Air Force canceled the program in 1957 because the missile was too slow to be useful against modern air defenses. That history makes it clear the notification isn’t describing a Cold War-era leftover; the designation appears to have been reused, whether as a placeholder or a formal label for something new, rather than referring to the original Crossbow. “S-300 Clone” is similarly undefined in any public Pentagon or industry documentation, and no other name for it has surfaced.
The most plausible explanation available comes from outside the official notification. Robert Hamilton, a retired U.S. Army colonel who now leads the Delphi Global Research Center, told PBS NewsHour that the United States and Ukraine have been working jointly either to modernize Ukraine’s aging stock of S-300 interceptor missiles or to develop a newer version of the missile with improved capability. Hamilton said he expects that upgraded system to become operational close to the end of 2026. Neither the State Department nor Ukraine’s government has confirmed that this effort is the same program referenced as “S-300 Clone” in Friday’s notification, but the timing and subject matter line up closely enough that the two appear connected.
The S-300 is a Soviet-designed, long-range surface-to-air missile system that Ukraine inherited in large numbers and has relied on throughout the war, alongside Western systems like the Patriot. Ukraine has faced a persistent shortage of S-300 interceptors because Russia is now the only producer of the original missile, making any American-backed alternative, cloned, modernized or newly built, a potentially significant addition to Ukraine’s ability to keep those launchers firing.
The State Department’s notification includes the standard language used in nearly all such filings: the sale would not require additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine, would not affect U.S. military readiness, and would not alter the basic military balance in the region. No offset agreement has been proposed so far; any such arrangement would be negotiated separately between Ukraine and whichever companies win the eventual contracts.
What remains unclear is what the S-300 Clone and GAM-67 items actually are, technically or physically. Congress has not yet completed its review, and neither Washington nor Kyiv has released further detail on the specifications, quantities, or delivery timeline for either item.

articles.title: South Korea rebuffs Trump: No troops for US war on Iran
articles.body:
South Korea rebuffs Trump: No troops for US war on Iran
TEHRAN — In a decisive stance reflecting growing domestic anti-war sentiment and strategic prudent realism, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung announced on Friday that Seoul will not deploy its armed forces to join the US war against Iran, effectively rejecting escalating demands from Washington to entangle the East Asian nation in its Middle Eastern conflict.
Speaking at a news conference in Seoul, President Lee stated in unambiguous terms that South Korea will not participate in combat operations or allow its military assets to be dragged into Washington’s military campaign.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee told reporters. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
However, the South Korean leader noted that his administration is currently reviewing potential non-combat measures limited strictly to safeguarding commercial navigation and energy supply lines in the region. Seoul currently maintains a naval footprint off the coast of Somalia dedicated to anti-piracy missions, a model some officials have suggested could be adapted to protect South Korean flag-ships.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people,” Lee added, attempting to balance domestic political pressure against Washington’s persistent arm-twisting.
The official refusal from Seoul comes amidst heightened friction between the long-standing military allies. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized South Korea for what he characterized as insufficient support for Washington’s war effort against Tehran. In an apparent retributive move that has alarmed defense analysts in Seoul, the Trump administration recently scaled back major joint military exercises between US and South Korean forces.
Despite Washington’s economic and military leverage, Seoul’s refusal underscores the severe domestic and geopolitical constraints facing South Korean policymakers as they navigate the fallout from the US-Israeli war of aggression in West Asia.
Widespread domestic opposition in Seoul
President Lee’s firm statement follows weeks of intense domestic backlash and mounting public outrage across South Korea. Defense authorities in Seoul had previously disclosed that a specialized fact-finding mission had been dispatched to assess maritime conditions around the strategic Strait of Hormuz—a move that triggered immediate alarm among civil society groups and anti-war activists.
Earlier this month, dozens of South Korean anti-war activists, civil society leaders, and ordinary citizens gathered directly across from the massive United States embassy compound in central Seoul. Demonstrators fiercely condemned Washington’s pressure on their government, framing the US campaign against Iran as an “illegal war” of aggression.
Unfurling banners and holding signs reading “Do not join a war of aggression,” the protesters voiced deep indignation over indications that political and military leaders in Seoul were contemplating a military “contribution” to the waterway’s security at the behest of the White House.
Directing their chants toward the presidential office, the crowd echoed a resounding plea reflecting broad public sentiment against foreign military entanglements: “We cannot send our young people into a sea of death!”
While defense spokespersons in Seoul attempted to cool public anger by maintaining that no final deployment decision had been made, the public outcry highlighted the immense political cost any military compliance with Washington would entail for the South Korean government.
Tehran’s firm warnings against coercion
The prospect of South Korean military involvement in the Persian Gulf had drawn strong and explicit warnings from diplomatic authorities in Tehran, who made it clear that any foreign intervention alongside hostile American forces would carry severe economic and diplomatic consequences.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei repeatedly emphasized that any operational involvement by third countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz would be viewed as direct participation in US aggression.
In a detailed statement published in the Korean language on his official X account on September 7, Baghaei highlighted the historic depth of bilateral relations between Tehran and Seoul. He noted that Iran and South Korea have maintained diplomatic and economic ties for more than 64 years, built upon a solid foundation of mutual respect and constructive cooperation. Tehran, he reiterated, has consistently attached high value to its friendly bonds with the South Korean people.
However, the Iranian spokesman clearly delineated the boundaries of peaceful engagement amid Washington’s blatant violations of international law. Baghaei stressed that the Iranian nation is exercising its inherent right to self-defense against acts of aggression and responding decisively to US war crimes targeting civilians.
Under such fraught circumstances, Baghaei warned, any operational participation or military presence by foreign forces in the Persian Gulf and the strategic Strait of Hormuz would constitute direct support for the aggressor.
Urging South Korean policymakers to maintain an independent foreign policy aligned with international law and long-term national interests rather than American adventurism, the spokesman emphasized that responsible nations must resist foreign coercion.
“No sovereign and responsible country will submit to US pressure and blackmail to collude in committing acts of aggression and heinous crimes against the great Iranian nation,” Baghaei pointed out.
Washington’s fracturing alliances
Seoul’s reluctance to be drawn into the conflict exposes the growing isolation of the United States as it attempts to construct an international coalition to bolster its campaign in West Asia. Allies in both Europe and East Asia have shown marked reluctance to sacrifice their own strategic security and commercial stability for a war widely viewed as illegal and strategically disastrous. Yet, South Korea’s explicit refusal to send combat forces illustrates that even Washington’s closest treaty allies are unwilling to blindly follow American directives into the Persian Gulf.
Quagmire of war
The current regional crisis traces its origins back to the unlawful military campaign launched on February 28, when the United States and Israel embarked on a coordinated, unprovoked assault against Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Conceived in Washington and Tel Aviv with the illusion of achieving a rapid and decisive breakthrough, the war of aggression has instead evolved over the past seven months into a crushing geopolitical and military quagmire for the aggressors.
Far from coercing the region into submission or forcing sovereign nations to fall in line, the US-Israeli campaign has fractured Washington’s global alliance system, severely disrupted international maritime trade, and driven global energy markets into turmoil. By threatening allies like South Korea with military and economic retaliation while attempting to force participation in an unlawful war, the United States has succeeded only in exposing the limits of its global influence and the catastrophic miscalculations that have characterized its regional doctrine from the outset.

articles.title: Lithuania has intelligence about possible Russian hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies

Lithuania has intelligence about possible Russian hybrid attacks against Ukraine's allies
Kyiv • UNN
Lithuania and Poland have similar intelligence about possible Russian hybrid attacks involving drones and missiles. They could be made to look like accidents.
Lithuania has intelligence indicating possible hybrid attacks by Russia against countries supporting Ukraine. The data coincides with information from Poland and other allies, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said, as reported by Delfi, writes UNN.
Details
The statement came after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of possible Russian hybrid strikes involving drones and missiles. According to him, Moscow may try to portray such incidents as accidental.
Budrys said that he had discussed this intelligence with NATO leadership and European military officials.
Lithuania considers a false flag operation possible
I wanted to make sure that we were talking about the same thing. Indeed – yes, we are talking about the same thing. Lithuania has the same information; we discussed it as a possible false flag operation by Russia

articles.title: Turkiye revokes operating licence of Iran’s Bank Mellat in Istanbul
articles.body:
Turkiye revokes operating licence of Iran’s Bank Mellat in Istanbul
The Iranian lender has faced years of Western sanctions over alleged ties to Tehran’s nuclear programme.
Turkiye’s banking watchdog has revoked the operating licence of Iranian lender Bank Mellat’s branch in the Turkish city of Istanbul.
“It has been decided to revoke the operating licence of Bank Mellat, Head Office in Tehran, Istanbul Turkey Central Branch,” read the decision by the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency (BDDK), published in the Official Gazette on Saturday.

The regulator said the decision was taken under a clause of Turkiye’s banking law allowing a bank’s licence to be revoked or withdrawn if its continued operation is deemed to pose a risk to depositors’ rights or to the security and stability of the financial system.
Bank Mellat has been subject to Western sanctions for years over accusations that Tehran was pursuing a nuclear weapon under the cover of a civil nuclear programme.
Those sanctions were lifted as part of a landmark 2015 deal between Tehran and world powers to curb Iran’s nuclear ambitions. However, the United States unilaterally pulled out of the agreement in May 2018, reimposing economic sanctions on the country.
Bank Mellat was hit by further US and Gulf sanctions in 2019 after being named as one of 25 entities linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The Turkish notice did not cite the US measures or specify operational issues.
Earlier this month, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on a small Turkish investment bank and two subsidiaries over alleged ties to Iran.
The Treasury Department accused Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi (Golden Global Bank) of facilitating “tens of millions of dollars’ worth of transactions for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force” and providing the Iranian government with banking access to move its funds internationally.
Golden Global Bank has denied the accusations.

articles.title: Switzerland Adopts Security Strategy to Counter Hybrid Threats
articles.body:
The Swiss Federal Council has approved a comprehensive new security strategy aimed at bolstering national defense capabilities, safeguarding critical infrastructure, and preparing the country against hybrid and standoff attacks amid deteriorating European security conditions driven by Russia’s war against Ukraine.
According to Anadolu Agency on Sept.18, the Swiss government stated that the global security landscape has grown increasingly volatile and unpredictable.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bern has identified escalating great-power rivalries, regional armed conflicts, the degradation of the international rules-based order, and a surge in hostile cyber operations and foreign influence campaigns as primary catalysts for the policy overhaul.
Swiss authorities underscored that an end to Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine remains nowhere in sight, while hybrid threats targeting European democracies continue to multiply and intensify across physical and digital domains.
Partner defense cooperation
The updated blueprint sets out 10 strategic goals and 46 specific operational measures. Under the framework, Switzerland plans to substantially elevate the resilience of state institutions, the domestic economy, and civil society, while systematically curbing critical external dependencies.
The strategy prioritizes reinforced protections for the civilian populace, constitutional bodies, and vital supply networks.
A central pillar of the new posture involves expanding conventional defense capabilities. The document mandates that the Swiss armed forces must maintain operational readiness to deter and counter potential armed aggression, directing defense planners to establish pre-arranged cooperative mechanisms with partner nations well before an active crisis erupts.
US Approves $2.68B Air Defense Equipment Sale to Ukraine
Federal authorities stressed that special focus must be directed toward the threats deemed most probable in the contemporary threat environment, specifically state-sponsored hybrid warfare, long-range standoff strikes, and transnational organized crime networks.
Implementation of several strategic measures has already commenced across federal departments. The State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS) will oversee and coordinate execution of the blueprint, with the Swiss Federal Council scheduled to receive its first comprehensive progress report by the end of 2028.
Alignment with EU sanctions
The adoption of the defense blueprint marks another milestone in Switzerland’s calibrated departure from strict historical neutrality in response to Moscow’s aggression on the continent.
In recent years, Bern has moved in lockstep with the EU to implement consecutive economic sanctions targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, energy revenues, and banking apparatus.
The Swiss government has enacted a total ban on the purchase and import of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) in February, aligning domestic regulations with the EU’s 19th sanctions package to curtail fossil fuel revenues financing the Kremlin’s war effort.
Alongside the energy restrictions, Swiss authorities prohibited domestic financial intermediaries from providing cryptocurrency services to Russian nationals and legal entities, while barring transactions involving ruble-backed crypto assets.
Bern has also expanded its statutory export control lists to restrict shipments of specialized industrial metals and advanced manufacturing components utilized in Russian weapon systems and domestic fuel production.

articles.title: South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
South Korea is rejecting pressure from the US to deploy its navy to the Strait of Hormuz, with President Lee Jae Myung saying on Friday he would not involve his country in the ongoing US-Iran war.
"There won't be [a] deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly," he told a press conference, adding that "we won't deploy military assets in any form to that end".
Lee did caveat the comments, saying that South Korea was reviewing playing a role in ensuring free navigation in the region.
"[It] is also clear we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people," he said.
Lee's comments come as commercial shipping around the Middle East, specifically in the Gulf and Red Sea, comes under increasing strain from both Iran and the Houthis as a means of exerting pressure on the global economy in response to the U/S-Israeli war launched in February.
This has directly affected South Korea, which imported 70% of its oil from the Gulf prior to the outbreak of the war, alongside significant portions of LNG.
It also comes amid threats from US President Donald Trump, who asked the country in August to "give us a hand" with Iran, later saying he would scale back military drills after South Korea said no.
He also questioned why South Korea would say no, given that tens of thousands of US troops are stationed in the country.
"We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbour. And you're not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran? That’s strange," he said.
Trump and members of his administration have also criticised European allies for not getting involved in the war.
The US has 28,500 troops stationed in South Korea, one of the longest continuous US military deployments, having been there since 1957.
Since the start of the war, the US has redeployed some forces out of the country, most importantly Patriot and THAAD batteries needed to intercept Iranian ballistic missiles.
Alongside Lee's comments, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
South Korea's foreign ministry said that Cho had explained to Rubio that the country would make a contribution to restoring freedom of navigation, though it didn't elaborate what this would look like.

The HUR showed the Japanese delegation components of a ballistic missile from North Korea
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian intelligence demonstrated components of a North Korean ballistic missile to the Japanese delegation. The details help assess Pyongyang's weapons.
Experts from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine demonstrated to the Japanese delegation components of a ballistic missile manufactured by North Korea, which make it possible to assess its characteristics and the capabilities of North Korea’s military-industrial complex. The missile components were shown to Speaker of the House of Representatives of the Parliament of Japan Eisuke Mori and other members of the Japanese delegation during their visit to Kyiv.
According to intelligence data, examining the components makes it possible to determine the missile’s technical characteristics, design features, and the level of development of North Korea’s defense industry.

North Korean weapons pose a threat not only to Ukraine, but also to Japan and other countries in the Asia-Pacific region

articles.title: What Russia attacked Ukraine with this night and how many targets were shot down

What Russia attacked Ukraine with this night and how many targets were shot down
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched two Tsirkon missiles and 174 drones. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 141 targets, but hits were recorded at 15 locations.
During the night of September 19, Russia attacked Ukraine with 2 Zircon anti-ship missiles and 174 strike and other drones, half of which were jet-powered Shaheds. Air defense forces shot down or suppressed 141 aerial targets, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported, according to UNN.
Details
The main directions of Russia’s attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions. The enemy launched the Zircon missiles from Russia’s Kursk region, and the drones from Oryol, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, and the temporarily occupied Donetsk and Crimea.
For the attack, Russia used Shaheds, Gerbera drones, Bandеrol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parody imitation drones. The aerial attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
How many targets air defense neutralized
As of 08:00, air defense had shot down or suppressed 138 Shahed-, Gerbera-, and other types of drones, as well as 3 Bandеrol/Dan-T munitions.
The Air Force recorded strikes by aerial attack weapons at 15 locations; at another 9 locations, downed targets or their debris fell. Neither of the two Zircon missiles reached its target; the locations where they fell are being clarified.
As of the time of publication of the report, the attack was ongoing—more than 10 enemy UAVs remained in Ukraine’s airspace.

articles.title: Trump Signs Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill, Putting New Pressure Tools At His Disposal
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump signed into law legislation aimed at increasing economic pressure on Russia over its war on Ukraine, including by targeting Moscow's energy revenues as well as countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
The White House said on September 18 that Trump signed H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- the legislation named after the late South Carolina senator who championed tougher measures against Moscow.
The signing makes the Russia sanctions measure law after it passed the Senate by an 86-11 vote in August and the House of Representatives by 262-159 on September 16.
The law gives the Trump administration sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions.
But much of its practical impact will depend on decisions by Trump and his administration.
Targeting Russian Energy Revenues, Sanctions Evasion
Among its most consequential provisions, the law authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods imported from countries that fall within specified categories tied to purchases of Russian oil and natural gas or the circumvention of US sanctions.
The legislation focuses in particular on five importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, which purchased the largest amounts of these commodities during the 12-month period preceding its enactment, as well as countries identified as major facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
The administration is required to reassess the countries covered by the provisions every 180 days.
The law also targets Russia's so-called shadow fleet -- the vessels and networks used to transport Russian energy and evade sanctions -- as well as foreign individuals and companies involved in supporting Russian energy production or sanctions evasion. The legislation can affect vessel owners, operators, managers, insurers, and other participants in activities within its scope.
The measure also contains provisions targeting major Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects, including Yamal LNG and Arctic LNG 2, large facilities in the Russian Arctic designed to produce and export the fuel.
At the same time, the law gives Trump considerable discretion over how and whether some of its powers are used. He can waive sanctions, restrictions, or duties if he determines that doing so is in the national interest and provides Congress with an explanation.
That means the signing itself does not automatically impose a 100 percent tariff on countries such as China or India. Rather, it gives the administration the statutory authority to impose such duties under specified circumstances.
The legislation also extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031.
Experts: Implementation Will Determine Impact
Daniel Fried, a former State Department sanctions coordinator, told RFE/RL on September 18 that Trump's decision to sign the measure was significant, but said the president had missed an opportunity to publicly use the moment to send a message to Moscow.
“It’s good that President Trump signed the bill into law,” Fried said. “But the lack of a public statement means that he has missed a chance to send a message to Putin that he needs to end the war.”
Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute who focuses on national security and transatlantic relations, said the legislation's symbolism was particularly important.
“One of the most important aspects of this new legislation is its symbolism and timing,” Coffey told RFE/RL.
He said the bipartisan support for the measure highlighted the role of Republicans in Congress, including lawmakers who had previously been skeptical about continued US involvement in Ukraine.
Coffey said he hoped the legislation could influence the debate among supporters of the Trump movement by demonstrating how support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia could be framed as being in US interests.
But he cautioned against expecting an immediate wave of new sanctions or tariffs.
“I would not expect major new sanctions or tariffs to be implemented overnight as a result of this legislation,” Coffey said.
Instead, he noted, the law codifies many existing sanctions, which he described as significant in itself.
Coffey also pointed to a provision that has received less attention: a restriction on US businesses pursuing new business deals or investments in Russia, or with Russian entities, until there is a peace agreement acceptable to Ukraine.
He said that provision could become particularly important because some political and business interests in Washington are waiting for an opportunity to restore commercial ties with Moscow.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the bipartisan vote was an encouraging signal for Ukraine and demonstrated continued congressional support for maintaining pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The bipartisan vote is an encouraging signal for Ukraine, and it shows our Congress still backs pressure on Putin across party lines,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
Tariffs have proved difficult to use against major purchasers of Russian energy, she cautioned.
She pointed to China's response to US tariffs in April 2025, when Beijing retaliated with tariffs of its own and restricted rare-earth exports.
“It will take resolve from the president and the American public to stick to the threat,” Bitsoff said.
She also pointed to the enforcement of sanctions already on the books as a key test of how the administration will use the new powers.
“There hasn't been movement from Treasury on the Russia sanctions already in place in almost eleven months,” she said. “Enforcement on those from Treasury will be a good indication of whether Trump will use this new authority or let it sit.”
Zelenskyy Welcomes Trump's Signature
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked Trump and members of Congress for backing the legislation, while invoking Graham's longstanding advocacy for maintaining pressure on Moscow.
“When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions, and seek a path to peace,” Zelenskyy said in a post to X.
He urged the administration to implement its provisions “fully and swiftly.”
“Peace comes through strength,” Zelenskyy said. “Calm comes through security. And the best guarantee of security is resolve.”

articles.title: Germany Top General Warns Country Must Prepare for Defense Amid Rising Russian Threats
articles.body:

Germany Top General Warns Country Must Prepare for Defense Amid Rising Russian Threats
Germany must mobilize its entire society, industry, and armed forces to prepare for national defense and the potential risk of war, according to Inspector General of the Bundeswehr Carsten Breuer, Bild reports on September 17.
Speaking at the IISS Prague Defense Summit, Germany's highest-ranking military officer emphasized that military strength and modern technology alone cannot protect the country against current security challenges.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Breuer noted that rapid technological advances cause military tactics to quickly become outdated. Because of this, according to Bild, he stated that Germany needs to closely study the combat experiences gained during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Russia learns. They copy and adapt, introducing innovations aimed at our strengths and bypassing them. Technology should not determine what we do. We must determine what we do with technology," the general stated.
He stressed that standing up to hybrid threats requires a broader response beyond the capabilities of the armed forces.
Addressing the German people, Breuer said, "Without you, we soldiers are doomed to fail. But failure is not an option. Because that would mean a fatal threat to our societies as we know them. We are all in the same boat."
Breuer had previously ordered the Bundeswehr to achieve full operational capability by 2029 to counter a potential Russian attack on NATO territory.
Funded through an easing of Germany’s constitutional debt brake, the directive prioritizes expanding air defenses, long-range precision strike capabilities, electronic warfare, and ammunition stockpiles following warnings that Russia could rebuild its forces to launch large-scale aggression by 2029.
Since the beginning of 2026, German authorities have recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases and 747 incidents involving suspicious drones near military sites and critical infrastructure.
Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle Airport incident, where an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft, and later announced the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least 11 and injure dozens over past 24 hours
articles.body:
The Ukrainian air force reported that Russian forces had fired two “Zircon” missiles as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight.
Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 11 people and injured dozens more over the past day, according to local authorities.
In Kharkiv Oblast in northeastern Ukraine, five people were killed and 15 were injured in Russian attacks, governor Oleh Syniehubov reported, adding that Russian forces had fired two missiles, five guided aerial bombs, and almost 60 drones at targets across the region.
Strikes reportedly hit the villages of Lypkuvativka, Velykyi Burluk, and Slatyne, as well as the cities of Kharkiv and Balakliia, among other locations.
Two people were also killed and five were wounded following a wave of drone attacks, air strikes, and artillery shelling across the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, per the Kherson Regional State Administration.
"Russian troops struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging, in particular, five high-rise buildings and seven private homes," it said in a statement posted on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed administrative buildings, stores, a cell tower, a utility building, a gas pipeline, and private vehicles".
In Donetsk in the east of the country, one person was killed in the city of Kramatorsk while 13 people were injured across the wider region.
A 51-year-old man and a 45-year-old woman were also killed after a guided missile struck a high-rise building in Sumy Oblast in the north, authorities said. A 32-year-old man also died following a drone attack in the region.
The Sumy Regional Military Administration reported 50 attacks on 21 settlements from Friday to Saturday morning, with Russian forces said to have launched drones, mortars, artillery, and guided aerial bombs.
It comes as the Ukrainian air force reported that Russia had fired two “Zircon” missiles from its Kursk region as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight.
"According to preliminary data, as of 8 am, air defence forces shot down or neutralized 141 targets," the force said, adding that strikes had been recorded at 15 locations.
On Saturday, Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said it had activated air defence measures and scrambled military aircraft in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine.
"These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in regions adjacent to threatened areas," it said in a statement.

articles.title: Moscow summons British envoy over weapons supplies to Ukraine
articles.body:
The Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Britain's chargé d'affaires in Moscow, Danae Dholakia, on Friday to issue a formal protest about what it called London's "further increase" in weapons supplies to Ukraine.
In a statement, the ministry said that by sending more arms to Kyiv, "London is placing itself in the position of an accomplice to the bloody atrocities committed by the Kyiv regime, which can only be characterized as terrorism and war crimes."
A spokesperson for Britain's Foreign Office called the summoning "yet another attempt to deflect attention from Russia's barbaric full-scale invasion of Ukraine and discredit the UK on the world stage."
Russia currently has no ambassador in London, and relations are dire.
The departure of the previous Russian ambassador, Andrei Kelin, in July prompted British media speculation - denied by Russia - that Moscow was downgrading diplomatic relations because of London's role as one of Ukraine's biggest supporters.
Poland joins anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine
Also on Friday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Poland has joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies.
"From today, Poland is part of this major project... we agreed on the forms and frameworks of this cooperation," Tusk said in a video posted on X/Twitter.
Tusk attended a summit on Friday of a new regional grouping of eight Carpathian countries, held in western Ukraine and launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Ukraine and nine European countries announced in July an air-defense coalition that would jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system as an alternative, cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.
Tusk told a press conference at the summit that Poland has prepared a new "significant" donation package for Ukraine, without giving further detail.
"I will be very consistent here. No one will change my opinion that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression... History cannot divide us vis-à-vis Russia today," Tusk said.
After his bilateral meeting with Tusk at the summit, Zelensky thanked Poland for the new aid package.
"Ukraine and Poland are strong neighbors, friends, and partners, and we have one common enemy," he said on the Telegram app.

articles.title: Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure
articles.body:
Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure
Former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
He noted that Ukraine has significantly increased its drone production during the years of the full-scale war, from several thousand to nearly 10 million annually. In the politician’s view, further scaling up these capabilities, combined with the development of missile systems, could fundamentally shift the balance of power.
Landsbergis stressed that building a comprehensive deterrence system requires not only weapons themselves but also the necessary infrastructure, including guidance systems and satellite capabilities.
“Add ballistic missiles to that. Good guidance systems, satellites and the like are also needed – to reach the point where, with or without allies, Ukraine can tell Putin: ‘Look, even if you try again next time, you will have no industry left,’” the politician said.
He believes Ukraine is uniquely positioned to establish such a system and that Western countries can help it achieve this.
“There is no other country that could do this – only Ukraine. And we, the West, are capable of helping Ukraine achieve it,” Landsbergis said.
At the same time, he believes Ukraine’s experience could also be used to strengthen the defenses of other countries potentially threatened by Russia.
Lithuania and other neighboring countries of Russia, in particular, could develop their own long-range deterrence systems adapted to their capabilities. According to the politician, this would allow countries in the region to rely not only on assistance from their allies but also on their own capabilities.
“That is what deterrence is – sovereign power,” Landsbergis emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 18, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced during his visit to Ukraine that Poland had joined the Antiballistic Coalition.

articles.title: US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump claims 'infinite' Greenland security deal with Denmark
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
Denmark and Greenland -- an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen -- both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.
"I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."
The 80-year-old said it was an "'Infinite Life' Agreement, there is no end!" and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.
'Good agreement'
Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland amid a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.
"This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors," a State Department official said.
At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen had said Monday that she was "optimistic" that ongoing discussions with the United States and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute.
On Friday, she said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," adding that it was "good for NATO and Europe."
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States "strengthens" the territory's security.
NATO tensions
Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal.
But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.
A 1951 defense pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.
Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.
(AFP)
