articles.title: Trump signs new Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
Trump signs new Russia sanctions bill
US President Donald Trump has signed sweeping legislation expanding the sanctions on Russia and authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. Moscow warned that additional sanctions would complicate efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict and could further destabilize the energy markets.
In a statement on Friday, the White House announced that Trump approved the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, after the Senate passed it 86-11 in August and the House passed it 262-159 on Wednesday.
The legislation targets senior Russian officials, banks, defense and energy entities, as well as what Western countries refer to as Russia’s ‘shadow fleet’ of ships. It also empowers Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas.
The text, however, does not explicitly name major Russian energy buyers such as China or India, and the tariff rate can be set below the 100% ceiling.
The measure was initially proposed by late Republican Senator and Russia hawk Lindsey Graham and Democrat Richard Blumenthal in April 2025. The original proposal threatened 500% tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy, but after more than a year of negotiations with the White House, the figure was cut to 100%.
The bill also grants Trump broad waiver powers, allowing him to suspend sanctions according to national interests and giving his administration wide leeway in setting tariff rates – one of the key points of negotiations between the White House and lawmakers, as some feared that the legislation would give Trump too much power.
The Trump administration recently eased sanctions on Russian oil. During the Iran war, the administration issued temporary exemptions allowing the sale and delivery of Russian oil already at sea to alleviate pressure on the energy markets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned on Thursday that the “unfriendly” move “would definitely complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington argued that blocking Russian energy trade while Middle Eastern supplies are disrupted could prove costly for the US, calling it an “invitation to ever-higher prices at the pump.” It also warned that simultaneously escalating tensions with Moscow and Beijing would be a geopolitical lose-lose situation and would “only play into the hands of Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”

articles.title: Latvian defence technology companies meet German industry leaders in Berlin
articles.body:
During a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Latvian defence and dual-use technology companies met leading German defence companies, industry organisations and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence in Berlin. Members of the delegation, led by Latvian Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis, presented their solutions and discussed opportunities to join German companies’ supply chains, jointly develop technologies and expand production.
The programme focusing on defence and dual-use technologies began on 16 September with an event dedicated to cooperation between the Latvian and German defence industries, organised in partnership with the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV).
“Industrial cooperation between Latvia and Germany is becoming increasingly close. In the first half of 2026, Latvia’s exports of goods to Germany grew by 10%, while exports of machinery, mechanical appliances and electrical equipment increased by EUR 34.3 million. This also represents the manufacturing base on which Latvia’s defence industry can grow. Our companies can supply electronic components, unmanned systems, military vehicles, metal structures and other solutions needed to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. The priority now is to involve Latvian companies more extensively in German and European supply chains, joint technology development and manufacturing,” Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis said.
Latvian business representatives met the leadership of BDSV, German defence companies and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence to discuss industry priorities, upcoming procurements and opportunities for cooperation.
Direct talks with the German defence industry
During an in-depth industry session, Rheinmetall, HENSOLDT, Rohde & Schwarz and Quantum Systems presented their expertise and opportunities for cooperation. Discussions focused on expanding defence production and supply chains, sensors, electronic warfare and counter-unmanned aerial system solutions, secure communications and autonomous systems.
Latvia’s defence technology ecosystem was presented to German partners by Artis Pabriks, Executive Director of the Military Technology, Drone and Robotics Association MilTech Latvia, and Jānis Atslēns, a representative of the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia.
“As Ambassador, security is one of my main priorities in relations between Latvia and Germany. We cooperate both bilaterally and as NATO and EU partners. Germany is one of the world’s leading military industry countries, and Latvia has excellent opportunities to develop closer cooperation with the German defence industry. We have highly qualified specialists and innovative companies capable of adapting to changing industry conditions. Trust and close professional contacts form the foundation of this type of long-term cooperation. The Embassy will continue to actively support Latvian companies by helping them establish new contacts, strengthen their presence in the German market and become part of the European defence industry’s supply chains,” said Ilze Rūse, Latvia’s Ambassador to Germany.
Focus on unmanned and autonomous systems
On 17 September, Latvian and German companies, industry organisations and public-sector representatives participated in a round-table discussion on unmanned aerial vehicles and counter-UAV technologies, autonomous systems, robotics, artificial intelligence, secure communications, electronics and the resilience of defence supply chains. The event was organised by LIAA in cooperation with Berlin’s economic development agency Berlin Partner and MilTech Latvia.
Participants were introduced to the Latvian and Berlin defence technology ecosystems, while Latvian and German companies presented their solutions. The discussions explored specific areas for cooperation, including component supplies, systems integration, joint product development, technology testing and manufacturing.
“Economic cooperation between Latvia and Germany already has a solid foundation, with more than 1,000 German-owned companies operating in Latvia. In the defence industry, Latvian companies must now demonstrate their ability to meet specific technical, quality and delivery requirements. In Berlin, they had an opportunity to discuss these matters with potential partners and determine what steps are necessary to qualify as suppliers. Following the mission, LIAA will continue working on the most promising cooperation opportunities, advancing them towards technology testing, supplier qualification and cooperation agreements,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
Berlin is strengthening its position on Europe’s defence and security technology map. The city is home to approximately 130 companies specialising in security and defence, as well as more than 400 companies whose technologies can be used for both civilian and military purposes. The Berlin Senate is also developing a dedicated defence technology ecosystem to forge closer links between companies, researchers, investors and public-sector customers.
The delegation also visited Andres Industries AG, a Berlin-based company that develops and manufactures thermal imaging and night-vision technologies for armed forces, police and other security institutions.
Latvian companies offer technologies and manufacturing capacity
The Latvian delegation of defence and dual-use technology companies included ALMIKO, Daugavpils Lokomotīvju Remonta Rūpnīca, Electrify, EMJ Metāls, HansaMatrix, Latvia Packing, VOLBURG, VORX and VR Cars.
The delegation’s offering encompasses printed circuit board and electronics manufacturing, metalworking and the production of armoured structures, military ammunition packaging, materials for large-format 3D printing, military vehicles and unmanned ground platforms. In Germany, Latvian companies are seeking systems integrators, customers, manufacturing partners and opportunities to participate in German and broader European defence projects.
For example, Electrify presented the Latvian-developed Rocky6 electric unmanned ground platform in Berlin. It is designed to transport cargo and specialised equipment across difficult terrain, perform reconnaissance, evacuate casualties, and integrate communications and counter-UAV systems. The platform has a payload capacity of up to 1,200 kilograms and an electric range of up to 150 kilometres.
“Latvian defence technology companies offer their German partners a powerful combination of flexibility, engineering expertise and solutions tailored to real operational needs. At DK NEJET, we develop software-defined defence technologies, ranging from high-speed interceptors and navigation in GPS-denied environments to drone-swarm coordination. We combine engineering development, manufacturing and operator training within a single ecosystem. Combined with Germany’s industrial capacity, this creates a solid foundation for the rapid deployment of field-tested and cost-effective European defence solutions,” said DK NEJET co-founder Olga Provotar, emphasising the importance of participating in LIAA’s trade mission to Germany.
Trade mission covers several technology sectors
The Latvian business trade mission to Germany, organised by LIAA, took place from 14 to 17 September. It brought together 53 Latvian companies and organisations representing information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, and defence and dual-use technologies. The programme was organised by sector, combining company visits and joint events with individual business meetings.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvia’s exports of goods and services to Germany have grown by more than 40%, rising from EUR 1.47 billion to approximately EUR 2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France and China combined.
Growth has continued this year: in the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, while Latvia’s total exports grew by 6%. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for service exports, which reached EUR 779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 German-owned companies operate in Latvia, with their combined investments in share capital exceeding EUR 800 million.
LIAA organises participation in international trade missions under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

articles.title: US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US-Israel arms transfers: 2,000 pound bombs, destruction in Gaza
The United States' approval of a $2.8bn arms deal with Israel has renewed criticism of US policy towards Tel Aviv, with the package set to include 2,000-pound bombs that have frequently been used in both Gaza and Lebanon to devastating effect.
The approval, which could bypass Congress, is set to replenish the stockpile of heavy munitions, according to reporting from the New York Times.
What are these munitions, where have they been used, and why have they spurred controversy? The New Arab takes a look.
Heavy munitions
The arms package consists of 40,000 heavy bombs developed and made by the US, including 20,000 MK-84 bombs and 20,000 BLU-117 bombs.
The bombs are nearly identical, weighing 2,000 pounds (907kg), creating up to 50 feet (15 metres) deep craters in use, as well as being programmed to detonate above ground as well as underground.
Detonation above ground can send shrapnel 1,000 feet (300 metres) in any direction.
Alongside the bombs, the US will also be supplying 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads. These bombs are also 2,000 pounds but are reinforced and explode on delay, allowing them to punch through surfaces before exploding underground.
Where have they been used?
These bombs have been extensively used by Israel in its wars on Gaza and Lebanon, to deadly effect.
Israel’s war on Gaza has killed over 73,000 Palestinians in a dense urban environment that saw Israeli strikes sometimes killing hundreds at a time in built-up areas, particularly during the first months of the war.
Their repeated use in Gaza, and Israel’s other wars, has seen the US resupply Israeli stockpiles several times in the last three years. In 2024, the Biden administration blocked the transfer of 2,000-pound bombs amid public pressure urging Washington to stop Israel’s invasion of Rafah, which occurred anyway.
US President Donald Trump later unblocked the transfer of the weapons, just a few days into his administration.
According to the New York Times, it has identified 208 craters at least 40 feet across in an area of southern Gaza where Israel told civilians to move to safety.
One such incident in the Jabaliya Refugee Camp at the start of the war killed around 195 Palestinians and wounded a further 777, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, which has since seen the systematic destruction of infrastructure in Israeli-occupied areas of the enclave, has destroyed most of Gaza’s housing and other infrastructure, including schools, hospitals, roads, water and sewage.
Though Israel has launched campaigns against seven Middle Eastern countries since the outbreak of its war on Gaza -- including Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iran, Iraq and Qatar – MK-84 bombs are not deep-strike munitions, meaning they have a minimum range that’s limited to the aircraft's operational range, limiting their usage to areas where Israeli aircraft can directly fly over.
Where is the backlash?
The sale has generated backlash from parts of the US political scene, which has seen figures from both sides of the aisle become increasingly wary of the partnership with Israel.
The most vocal critic of the deal among the Democrats has been Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and supporter of Israel, who said he would not clear Trump’s proposal.
In a press release published on Wednesday, Meeks said that though he is committed to Israel’s security, “the Trump administration’s proposed sale of 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, some of the most destructive munitions in our arsenal, raises grave, unresolved concerns about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon".
“The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with U.S. law and with appropriate protections for civilians. I therefore will not clear this sale at this time,” he added.
Democrat Senator Chris Van Hollen also weighed in on X, saying he would work to stop the transfer.
Within the Republican political commentariat, Tucker Carlson, who in recent years has distinguished himself as a staunch critic of Israel’s wars in the region, also hit out against the decision.
“By definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide. The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region.
“If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do,” he added.
It is unlikely that Congress will be able to stop the transfer, as it would require a resolution of disapproval with a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate, which has never happened before, according to the New York Times.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations have also bypassed congressional reviews when selling and transferring arms to Israel since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza by invoking emergency authority.

articles.title: Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
articles.body:
Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
Germany received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago from Lockheed Martin.
Germany has received its first F-35A Lightning II fighter jet, as the country accelerates a major military buildup and increases defence spending amid a broader push by European NATO members to strengthen their armed forces.
The delivery on Friday is part of Germany’s effort to fulfil NATO nuclear-sharing duties and modernise its military after decades of relatively low defence spending.
Lockheed Martin formally presented the aircraft to the German government during a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, attended by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius.
“This is the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force: the new F-35A fighter jet is the world’s most advanced combat aircraft,” Pistorius said in a statement. “It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology.”
Germany ordered 35 F-35As in 2022, the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The aircraft are intended to replace Germany’s ageing Tornado fleet.
The Trump administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defence, allowing Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.
European countries, including Germany, are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump’s demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

articles.title: US probes possible espionage after F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong: Report
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 September 2026•Update: 18 September 2026
Sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong this summer, prompting a congressional inquiry and concerns that China could gain access to components of the highly classified weapons system, Politico reported Friday.
A shipment of F-35 parts being sent from Australia to the US for repairs was rerouted while crossing the Pacific, according to the report. The Pentagon reportedly confirmed that some components had gone missing.
Anadolu separately contacted the Pentagon seeking confirmation and further details about the incident but had not received a response at the time of publication.
According to Politico, the parts were being transported by an intermediary for F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin but ultimately arrived in Hong Kong. It remains unclear why they were diverted or who currently possesses them, the report said.
The incident prompted ongoing briefings for congressional staff serving on key national security committees. State Department and Pentagon officials began briefing staff in June, with further briefings expected, it added.
Among the shipment’s contents was an F-35 canopy, which covers the cockpit and incorporates stealth technology available only to the US and its allies, according to the report. If obtained by an adversary, the components could potentially be studied and reverse-engineered.
The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Program Office said it was “aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components.”
The office said it is working with US authorities and industry partners “to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence.”
Because Hong Kong is a Chinese special administrative region, the diversion potentially placed the equipment within Beijing’s sphere of influence, according to the report.
China has also conducted espionage targeting classified Pentagon programs, including the F-35, the report said.
“It’s no secret that China has been aggressively trying to get F-35 data through electronic espionage, among other means,” J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staff member, was quoted as saying.
“But even if they already had specifications or other data about the part, possessing a real one can give them even more to go on and can verify or refine whatever they already had learned.”

articles.title: Russia reportedly buries its drone factory underground
articles.body:
- Ukrainian analyst Dnipro Osint said Russia has built about 42,000 square meters of underground production space for Shahed/Geran drones at Alabuga.
- The claim follows confirmed satellite evidence of new production halls, a 340-hectare site expansion, and defensive towers built around the facility in 2026.
Russia has begun building underground production space for its Shahed and Geran attack drones at the Alabuga industrial zone in Tatarstan, according to Ukrainian open-source intelligence analyst Dnipro Osint, who estimated roughly 42,000 square meters of underground area has already been constructed there.
Dnipro Osint said the shift underground appears to have followed earlier Ukrainian strikes on the Alabuga site, and that Russia has been expanding the underground infrastructure quickly since then.
The analyst placed the activity at coordinates 55.808719°, 52.026664°, within the broader Alabuga Special Economic Zone near the city of Yelabuga, roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) from the Ukrainian border. This specific underground construction claim comes from a single open-source analyst and has not yet been independently confirmed through separate satellite imagery analysis.
Alabuga is Russia’s primary production site for the Geran-2, a Russian-built version of Iran’s Shahed-136 one-way attack drone that Russian forces fire at Ukrainian cities on a near-nightly basis. The facility has grown substantially over the past year. Satellite imagery cited by Radio Liberty showed the zone’s footprint expanded by 340 hectares between May 2025 and May 2026, with new hangars, dormitories for foreign workers, and a roughly 450-hectare construction area added south of the M-12 highway. Ukrainian analysts reported on Sept. 14 that five additional production halls had gone up in the southern part of the site, based on satellite images similarly sourced from Dnipro Osint.
Russia has also added physical protection around the plant. Satellite images from July and August analyzed by Spencer Faragasso of the Institute for Science and International Security showed a two-ring system of lattice towers under construction around Alabuga’s production buildings, an arrangement meant to complicate future drone or missile strikes on the site.
Dnipro Osint said the combined effect of these changes, underground construction, dispersed production buildings and added physical defenses, is making Russia’s drone manufacturing base progressively harder and more expensive to target. The site relies heavily on foreign labor recruited through the Alabuga Polytechnic College and other channels; the United Kingdom sanctioned 35 entities and individuals in May 2026 over recruitment tied to the facility, and the site remains under separate U.S. and European Union sanctions.

articles.title: Russia’s next-gen Armata tank remains stuck a decade after debut
articles.body:
- New dashcam footage this week showed a Russian T-14 Armata tank crossing toward a firing range, with no new program details released.
- Russia has built roughly 20 T-14s against an original 2,300-tank target, and continues to rely on upgraded T-90M tanks for the war in Ukraine.
New dashcam footage circulating on Russian state-aligned media this week shows a T-14 Armata tank crossing a dirt road toward a firing range, the latest glimpse of a next-generation tank program that has spent a decade struggling to move beyond testing.
No new technical details accompanied the footage, and it does not appear to show anything beyond a routine range exercise. The clip, recorded from a passing civilian vehicle’s dashcam, adds to a long pattern of brief, unofficial sightings that have periodically resurfaced online since the T-14 was first unveiled during rehearsals for Russia’s 2015 Victory Day parade.
The T-14 represented a sharp break from Soviet-era tank design when Uralvagonzavod introduced it, built around an unmanned turret, a separately armored crew capsule, and the Afghanit active protection system meant to intercept incoming projectiles before they hit the vehicle. Russia originally planned to build more than 2,300 of the tanks by 2020. A decade later, estimates put the actual number built at roughly 20, most of them prototypes or pre-production vehicles rather than a true production run.
Cost has been the central obstacle. Estimates for the T-14 range from about $8 million to $15 million per vehicle, compared with $1.5 million to $2.5 million for an upgraded T-90M, the tank Russia has relied on instead throughout its war in Ukraine. Despite repeated claims from Russian officials and pro-government media that the T-14 has seen combat, no independently verified evidence has emerged confirming it ever fought at the front. Russian media reported in mid-2023 that a small number of Armatas reached Ukraine and fired from standoff range before being withdrawn within months, but outside analysts were never able to confirm those claims. British defense intelligence assessed at the time that Russian troops were reluctant to accept the tanks into service and that any deployment would likely serve propaganda purposes rather than combat need.
Even Rostec, the state conglomerate that oversees the T-14’s development, has acknowledged the program’s limits. Rostec chief executive Sergey Chemezov told Russian state news agency in March 2024 that while the Armata outperformed everything else in Russia’s inventory, it was too expensive to field at scale, and that the war would instead be fought with upgraded T-90Ms and refurbished T-72s. Uralvagonzavod, the world’s largest tank plant and the T-14’s manufacturer, has since turned much of its production capacity toward exactly that work, rebuilding older T-72 hulls and building new T-90Ms rather than expanding Armata output.
Some Russian defense industry figures have floated a different path forward, arguing that individual technologies developed for the T-14, its firepower, protection or mobility systems, could be transferred into the more widely fielded T-90M and T-72 rather than fielding the Armata itself in large numbers. Russia has also offered to transfer T-14 technology to India for local production under that country’s domestic manufacturing program, though that arrangement has not produced any confirmed manufacturing to date.
Analysts who track the program have grown increasingly skeptical of its future. Long development timelines and design choices that outside experts say have not kept pace with battlefield lessons from Ukraine have led some to describe the Armata as functionally dead on arrival as a mass-production tank, even as isolated footage like this week’s clip keeps the program in public view.

articles.title: Ukraine destroys Russian S-400 launcher in Bryansk region
articles.body:
- Ukraine's Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 launcher near Poroshino, Bryansk Oblast, on Sept. 17 using Fire Point's FP-1 drones.
- Fire Point said the launcher had been modified to strike ground targets, including Kyiv, and Ukraine's General Staff separately reported striking two S-400 launchers in the same region.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed a Russian S-400 air defense launcher in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on Sept. 17, using FP-1 drones, according to Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that builds the drone.
Fire Point said the launcher had been modified by Russian forces to strike ground targets and had previously been used against Kyiv. The company said the strike hit the launcher near the village of Poroshino, along highway 15K-303. The open-source monitoring group CyberBoroshno said it geolocated the destroyed vehicle from photos of the wreckage, pinning the site at coordinates 53.134224, 33.944510.
Ukraine’s General Staff separately reported that its forces struck two S-400 launchers overnight into Sept. 17 in the Vygonychi area of Bryansk Oblast, a location close to Poroshino, though it is not clear whether that report describes the same launcher Fire Point identified or a separate one. Russia has not confirmed any S-400 losses. Bryansk’s acting governor, Alexander Bogomaz’s successor Yegor Kovalchuk, said Russian air defenses shot down 82 drones over the region in 24 hours but made no mention of losses among the region’s own air defense systems.
The S-400 Triumf is Russia’s long- and medium-range surface-to-air missile system, built to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles, and Russia has claimed it can also intercept some ballistic targets. Since 2024, Russia has adapted some of the system’s interceptor missiles for a secondary role, firing them at ground targets in Ukraine on a quasi-ballistic trajectory. That dual use is why destroying individual launchers has become a specific target set for Ukraine, since a single system removed from service can eliminate both an air-defense asset and a launcher capable of hitting cities like Kyiv.
Fire Point introduced the FP-1 in late 2024 as a long-range, one-way attack drone built for deep strikes into Russian territory, with a payload of 60 to 120 kilograms (130 to 265 pounds) and a publicly stated range that has grown over time, from roughly 1,600 km (994 miles) at introduction to as much as 3,400 km (2,110 miles) in extended-range configurations the company began advertising in mid-2026.
The drone has previously been used against Russian refineries and other high-value sites well beyond the front line, including a strike on the Omsk refinery in July and a facility in the Yamalo-Nenets region on Sept. 9.

articles.title: 313,000  “Janfada” for Iran
articles.body:
313,000 “Janfada” for Iran
Tehran stages a defiant display of sacrifice and unity
TEHRAN — From Imam Hussein Square to Enghelab Square, Tehran’s streets on Friday became the setting for one of the largest public mobilizations seen in Iran since the war began in February. Hundreds of thousands of people took part in the “Janfada-ye Iran” — Devoted to Iran — campaign, with women, young people, veterans and other sections of society joining a 313,000-strong parade, according to Iranian organizers.
The scale of the gathering was matched by the symbolism surrounding it. Participants marched under Iranian flags, military banners and images associated with the country’s wartime resistance. Iranian drones and other military equipment were displayed along the route, while veterans of the Sacred Defense and volunteers in military-style formations took part in the parade. Some participants wore white burial shrouds — a stark traditional symbol of readiness to give one's life for the country.
The photographs from Tehran captured the atmosphere from different angles. In one image, a woman in camouflage and a green headband is seen positioned beside a vehicle, looking through the sight of a rifle. In another, a woman with her face partially covered by a patterned scarf holds an assault rifle while other women stand behind her amid Iranian and other flags. The images offer a striking visual of the campaign's central message: that the call to defend the country is being presented not solely through conventional military formations, but also through the participation of civilians, including women.
313,000: A number loaded with history
The choice of 313,000 is not simply a numerical designation.
In Islamic tradition, 313 is associated with the companions of the Prophet Muhammad at the Battle of Badr in 624 CE and, in Shiite tradition, with the number of devoted companions associated with the Imam of the Age. For the organizers of Friday's event, the number therefore carries a religious and historical meaning of steadfastness, loyalty and readiness to stand with a cause at a moment of crisis.
That symbolism was visible throughout the rally. The parade was not presented merely as a military exercise but as a public declaration of readiness, with participants repeatedly invoking the ideas of homeland, independence, national unity and sacrifice.
According to Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, commander of the Greater Tehran Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), around 500,000 people had registered in Tehran for the initiative. Iranian organizers have separately said that more than 31 million people have registered nationwide, while other Iranian reports put the cumulative figure above 32 million.
A rally born in wartime
What gives the Janfada campaign its particular character is the circumstances in which it has developed.
The campaign began on March 29, following the US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28, and has since evolved from a registration drive into a nationwide mobilization involving public gatherings, volunteer organization and preparations for training. Iranian officials say the volunteers are being organized into formations capable of contributing to national defense and other emergency tasks.
Friday's rally therefore came against the backdrop not of a distant or concluded war, but of an ongoing conflict, economic pressure and severe restrictions on Iran's trade and access to international markets. Recent reporting has also documented the effects of the US blockade and sanctions on Iran's economy and commercial routes.
This is an important distinction when placing the gathering in historical perspective. Across history, societies have mobilized around the idea of sacrifice when confronted by an existential military threat — from the Greek defenders at Thermopylae and the Soviet defense of Stalingrad to the French Resistance during World War II and Iran's own mass mobilization during the 1980–88 Iran-Iraq War.
But Janfada is being organized under a different set of circumstances. It combines a modern state-wide registration campaign, social-media mobilization, religious symbolism, and military-style public exercises while the conflict itself is still unfolding and while the country is simultaneously confronting economic pressure.
It is this combination that has given the campaign much of its political and social significance inside Iran.
Women, youth and veterans in the same formation
The Friday parade also sought to project an image of participation across generations.
Women appeared prominently in the event, including women in military-style uniforms and others carrying rifles. Young people took part alongside veterans of the Sacred Defense. Newly engaged couples were also reported among the participants, while a Jewish rabbi and a Yemeni delegation wearing traditional clothing were present, according to Iranian media reports.
President Masoud Pezeshkian, who attended the gathering, emphasized this diversity in his remarks. He described the turnout as a manifestation of the bond between the Iranian people and their homeland and stressed that “Iran belongs to all Iranians.” He called for unity and broad public participation in preserving 'the country's dignity, independence and territorial integrity.'
The message was significant: the campaign was being presented not simply as a gathering of members of Iran's military or paramilitary organizations, but as a national mobilization cutting across different sections of society.
From the 'Sacred Defense' to a new generation
Iran's modern experience of mass mobilization is inseparable from the Iran-Iraq War, known in Iran as the Sacred Defense.
During that eight-year conflict, Iran mobilized large numbers of volunteers through the Basij and other wartime structures. For an entire generation, the experience created a cultural vocabulary in which sacrifice, martyrdom, national defense and civilian participation became closely intertwined.
The Janfada campaign draws on that historical memory while speaking to a new generation.
The images from Tehran are particularly revealing in this respect. The rifles, uniforms and military vehicles evoke the visual language of wartime mobilization, while the presence of young people and women gives the event a distinctly contemporary character. The burial shrouds worn by some participants add another layer: rather than presenting sacrifice as an abstract concept, the participants were visually associating themselves with the possibility of death in defense of their country.
A message beyond Tehran
The significance of Friday's gathering also extends beyond the capital.
Iranian officials have said that Janfada gatherings are taking place in cities across the country and that the campaign is moving toward the organization and training of volunteer units. Basij chief Hossein Taeb said the volunteers were being prepared for “full-fledged defense,” while Iranian reports said training programs were being developed across ground, air and naval domains.
The campaign has consequently become both a domestic mobilization and an international signal.
For Tehran, the message is that the country's capacity to organize people around national defense has not disappeared under the weight of war, sanctions and economic pressure. The government is presenting the turnout as evidence of national resilience and social cohesion.
When a nation says it is ready
The most powerful element of Friday's scenes may not have been the military hardware displayed along Tehran's streets. It was the human presence surrounding it.
A woman holding a rifle. A veteran marches beside younger volunteers. Families moving through the crowd. Participants wearing burial shrouds. Flags rising above a sea of people stretching through one of Tehran's historic arteries.
For Iran, the language of Janfada reaches deep into a historical memory in which the survival of the homeland has repeatedly been associated with endurance and sacrifice.
Yet this time the setting is different. The pledge is being made while war is still being fought, while economic pressure is intensifying.
That is what makes the September 18 rally more than a single day's parade. It is the latest chapter in a campaign that seeks to transform the idea of sacrifice into an organized form of public participation — and to demonstrate, in the heart of Tehran, that the war has not removed the country's ability to mobilize large numbers of people around the defense of Iran.

articles.title: US troop deaths during Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four
articles.body:
US troop deaths during Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four
WASHINGTON – More US troops have died during the US-Israeli war with Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed, the Washington Post reported on Sept 18.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth denied the report.
The Post, citing five unidentified officials, reported that there had been at least 22 military fatalities, four more than were listed in the data available on the Pentagon’s public database.
The newspaper also reported, citing another unidentified official, that not all of the undisclosed deaths were directly tied to the months-long conflict but involved US personnel who were in the Middle East amid ongoing hostilities.
Hegseth, in a post on social media platform X, called the report “a complete LIE”.
The Post did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In its story, the newspaper said the Pentagon had declined to address its questions about the discrepancy in casualty accounting. REUTERS

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff pressed Russian leader Vladimir Putin during September talks in Moscow over his failure to capture Ukraine’s Donetsk region as previously claimed, according to report from The New York Times citing a source familiar with the discussions and a US administration official.

Russia plans to legalize at least 27 Yemeni citizens and then recruit them for the war against Ukraine. Some of them were born in 2006–2007.

articles.title: America’s strategy: lower costs and remote management
articles.body:
America’s strategy: lower costs and remote management
The Iran newspaper analyzed the United States’ current regional strategy. According to the paper, regardless of the outcome of the war with Iran, Washington appears intent on reducing its security commitments and costs in the region.
The formation of agreements such as the Mecca Pact can be interpreted within this framework. At the same time, the US is increasingly focused on containing China and the Asia-Pacific, preferring to manage regional developments remotely rather than through direct presence. Within this approach, the US seeks to turn the region into a space where rivals such as Iran, Russia, and China incur greater costs, rather than a theater for Washington’s own direct and expensive intervention. Rising energy costs for China and Europe are also seen as outcomes that could benefit the US. From this perspective, the naval blockade can be understood as a measure aimed at increasing pressure and gradually eroding Iran—pressure pursued without dragging the US into a large-scale, costly war.
Ettelaat: Tehran’s role in the emerging global economic order
Ettelaat examined President Pezeshkian’s participation in the 18th BRICS Summit in India. His presence—amid the US and Israeli-imposed war against Iran—offered a significant opportunity to strengthen Iran’s position within a multipolar order, expand economic diplomacy, and present a strong, active, constructive image of the country. The success of this engagement depends on internal coordination, managing expectations, focusing on practical projects, and reinforcing a positive, hopeful discourse. The event can be viewed as a “victory for development diplomacy.” Global gatherings such as BRICS, which bring together major and emerging powers from several continents, provide an ideal platform for expressing Iran’s stance regarding the imposed conflict. While appreciating BRICS’ statement condemning US and Israeli military aggression against Iran, the paper argues that Iran must make optimal use of this opportunity—especially in economic and financial domains.
Arman-e-Melli: A highly significant trip to Beijing
Arman-e-Melli highlighted the importance of Abbas Araghchi’s trip to Beijing amid regional tensions. According to the paper, what matters in analyzing current developments is this visit by Iran’s foreign minister. Given that Saudi Arabia canceled the planned Oman meeting, many analysts link Beijing’s selection as the destination to China’s potential mediation between Iran and Saudi Arabia. Whether these two matters are directly connected remains speculative, but China has adopted principled positions on regional developments in recent months. For this reason, some believe China may soon engage directly and effectively in regional dynamics.
Ham-Mihan: Failure in the Muscat meeting
Ham-Mihan, in an interview with foreign policy analyst Mohsen Jalilvand, explored the reasons behind the failure to hold the Muscat meeting. He argues it was clear from the outset that such a meeting would either not convene or, if held, would produce no tangible results—because the main actors, especially the United States and Israel, were absent from the negotiating table. Even if Tehran and Muscat reached a bilateral agreement on navigation protocols, the absence of defined and enforceable military deterrence boundaries or maritime transit arrangements means no deep strategic shift would occur. The international significance of the Strait of Hormuz stems from the fact that any change in its status is directly tied to the balance of power between Iran and the US, as well as broader Middle Eastern security dynamics. Although Persian Gulf states suffer the greatest economic vulnerability from shipping insecurity, they do not hold the final decision-making leverage. Therefore, technical agreements between Tehran and Muscat alone cannot resolve the current deadlock.

articles.title: Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
articles.body:
Explainer-How Putin may leverage predictable outcome of Russia's elections
MOSCOW, Sept 18 - Russians are voting in a three-day parliamentary election which is widely expected to see the ruling United Russia party retain its dominance in what is a tightly controlled political system that has excluded most candidates who oppose Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Even though the overall outcome is not in doubt, here are some of the reasons why the vote may be useful to President Vladimir Putin.
A MANDATE FOR MORE WAR?
As president or prime minister for more than a quarter of a century, Putin's grip on Russia has never been tighter. But the war has lasted much longer than many Russians expected and fallout from the conflict is now being felt much more sharply on the home front.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia itself have escalated, and while civilian casualties are far lower than in Ukraine, they have sharply increased this year. Strikes on oil refineries have caused fuel shortages, while businesses are grappling with drone attacks on their warehouses and polls suggest some Russians are increasingly anxious.
Having framed the election as a test of support for the war, Putin is likely to point to the results to say that most people back his decision to fight on until key war aims are met.
CREATION OF A 'NEW ELITE'
Putin has said that those who fought in Ukraine are "warriors", part of a new "elite" he has promised will have prestigious careers. Should the some 200 veterans standing from a range of parties do well, Putin is expected to point to their success at the ballot box as an example of how Moscow looks after those who risked their lives for the motherland and to show how distinguishing oneself on the battlefield can lead to a high-profile political career. It's a development that could also encourage more people to sign up to fight in Ukraine.
CONTRAST WITH UKRAINE
Putin has repeatedly suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is illegitimate, pointing to the fact that his five-year term ran out in May 2024 and that Zelenskiy has refused to hold a new election since. Martial law, introduced in Ukraine in 2022, bans any wartime election and the constitution says the president serves until a newly elected one takes office. But Putin - who has faced criticism from Western politicians about Russia's own political system - may use the vote to say that Russia - unlike Ukraine - has stuck to its electoral timetable regardless of the war and is giving people a chance to vote.
SENSE OF NORMALCY
Putin has been keen to show Russians that despite the conflict and everything associated with it they can largely carry on life as before. Increasingly deep and destructive Ukrainian drone strikes have made that harder to achieve in what is the fifth year of the war. But holding a relatively smooth parliamentary election across 11 time zones in what is the world's largest country, whilst also waging war in Ukraine, could help Putin reassure Russians that pre-war traditions are being respected and that life - up to a point - goes on despite the conflict.
MOBILISATION/CENSORSHIP
Putin this month dismissed suggestions by Ukraine and Western media pundits that Russia would carry out a post-election mobilisation to expand the ranks of its army in Ukraine as "nonsense," suggesting it was a malicious suggestion designed to sow panic.
However, domestic and foreign critics of the war fear he could use the outcome of the election to justify such a move, given what Western intelligence agencies say are heavy Russian losses on the battlefield and what they say is Moscow's desire to urgently speed up the pace of its territorial gains with more manpower.
Those same critics fear that the authorities may move ahead with more repressive measures once the election results are in and a pre-election feel-good mood is no longer required.
They point in particular to plans previously floated by the authorities to have mobile service providers charge customers extra for using more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data in a month, a move seen as targeting people who use VPNs or virtual private networks to access websites and apps banned inside Russia. The authorities have given no public indication they intend to imminently resurrect the plan. REUTERS

articles.title: Sybiha on Trump signing Graham Sanctioning Russia Act: Truly historic day
articles.body:
Sybiha on Trump signing Graham Sanctioning Russia Act: Truly historic day
The head of Ukrainian diplomacy wrote this on X, Ukrinform reports.
"A truly historic day. The Kremlin's calculations are failing once again. Pressure on Russia will only intensify, and Putin's hopes of weakening international support for Ukraine will fail," Sybiha emphasized.
He explained that President Trump's signing of the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran" would increase pressure on Russia and those who facilitate its war against Ukraine. It would further "isolate the aggressor and reduce the resources" fueling the war.
The minister noted that the law, adopted with "overwhelming bipartisan support in both chambers of Congress," sends a clear message: "the aggressor will pay a heavy price."
"We deeply appreciate the strong bipartisan support for Ukraine in the United States and honor Senator Lindsey Graham's commitment to peace and justice," Sybiha stressed.
The foreign minister added that Ukraine expects further decisive steps from partners in the EU and other G7 countries.

articles.title: Zelensky thanks Trump and America for implementing 'Graham Sanctioning Russia act'
articles.body:
Zelensky thanks Trump and America for implementing 'Graham Sanctioning Russia act'
The President of Ukraine published the relevant post on Telegram, Ukrinform reports.
"When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions and seek a path to peace. In particular, in those capitals that choose to buy Russian oil, provide financial services to Russia, and allow Russian companies linked to Putin and the war to engage in normal business relations in other countries," he wrote.
According to Zelensky, Senator Graham never doubted that America had enough strength to fight dictators and achieve results if it acted correctly.
The head of the Ukrainian state expressed gratitude to U.S. President Trump for signing this extremely important law. He also thanked all senators and members of the House of Representatives who supported it.

And the best reward for everyone helping us put pressure on Russia to end its war will be peace. Peace – and an end to all the problems and challenges this war has brought. Peace comes through strength. Calm comes through security. And the best guarantee of security is resolve. I thank everyone who resolutely defends life! I thank everyone who stands with Ukraine! America, thank you!" Zelensky emphasized.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 20 Chinese military aircraft and 14 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 20 Chinese military aircraft, 11 naval vessels and three official ships between 6 a.m. on Friday and the same time Saturday.
In response, aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems were deployed. Thirteen of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central, southwestern and eastern air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
So far this month, the defense ministry has tracked Chinese aircraft 175 times and ships 186 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Britain exploring return to making its own reactor fuel
articles.body:
Britain has begun exploring options to re-establish the production of reactor fuel for defence purposes, work the government says would be fully consistent with its obligations under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, according to the annual update to Parliament published this week.
The Nuclear Fuels Programme is part of the recapitalisation the Defence Nuclear Enterprise is carrying out simultaneously, which the update describes as covering two submarine build programmes with a further one in design, two warhead programmes, the fuel cycle work, and the infrastructure required to build and maintain those capabilities.
Every British submarine is nuclear powered, with the reactors manufactured by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Raynesway near Derby. The update describes nuclear propulsion as critical to sustaining continuous at sea deterrence, allowing submarines to remain dived on long-range patrols without detection.
Raynesway is one of the two sites receiving a share of the £6 billion committed under the Defence Investment Plan for infrastructure, alongside Barrow-in-Furness, investment the update says will grow the capability of the enterprise to produce a submarine every eighteen months in future.
Britain last enriched uranium for defence purposes at Capenhurst, and the country has relied on existing stocks for reactor fuel since domestic production ceased, which is the position the exploration now under way would change.
The update sets out the rest of the submarine picture alongside it. The Royal Navy has operated the Vanguard class since 1993, and those boats will be replaced by the Dreadnought class, with steel cut for the fourth and final Dreadnought in September 2025 on the same day the King commissioned HMS Agamemnon, the sixth Astute-class submarine.
The Astute class supports the deterrent while also undertaking other defence and intelligence tasks, including work with maritime task groups. Beyond those two programmes sits SSN-AUKUS, the design now in progress, with BAE Systems, the Defence Nuclear Organisation, Babcock and Rolls-Royce Submarines all maintaining teams at Barrow contributing to it.
The enterprise spent £12 billion in the 2025/26 financial year and projects spend of over £100 billion through British suppliers over the next ten years, with in excess of £20 billion more going into it between 2026/27 and 2029/30 than across the previous four years.

articles.title: Global: Amid mounting threats, the UN’s next Secretary-General must be a staunch defender of international law
articles.body:
Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard will be in New York City for the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly from September 22 to 26 and available for interviews. She will be meeting with senior UN figures and focusing her visit on the following issues:
- The selection of the next UN Secretary-General, and the state of the UN, multilateralism and the rules-based order
- Artificial Intelligence and the need for a global, binding, transparent, and effective regulatory model
- The Trump administration’s continuing attacks on international justice institutions
- International and multilateral responses to Israel’s genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank
- US-Israeli unlawful attacks on Iran, violations of international law and war crimes
- Iran’s internal repression, including crimes against humanity
- Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine
- Sudan, the role of the UAE and the international community
- DRC, critical minerals and Rwanda
“The United Nations is at one of its most critical junctures since its foundation more than eight decades ago. The world is beset by genocide, war, climate collapse, rampant inequality, ascendent anti-rights movements, unprecedented corporate power, and a reckless, unrestrained and extractive race to develop ever-more advanced AI. The Security Council is mired in paralysis while powerful states are further undermining the UN’s relevance and effectiveness by subjecting it to severe political, financial, and diplomatic pressure,” said Agnès Callamard.
“The next UN Secretary-General must be a staunch defender of international law. They must be willing to confront the powerful bullies and predators that stalk the international stage. They must be prepared to resist geopolitical pressure, condemn atrocities no matter who commits them, and engage meaningfully and constructively with civil society. They cannot simply be a consensus manager whose selection is the result of a closed-door compromise by the powerful. The next Secretary-General must be someone with the conviction and the know-how to mount a robust and effective defence of human rights and the UN Charter.”
The United Nations is at one of its most critical junctures since its foundation more than eight decades ago.

articles.title: Ukraine will receive new missiles for S-300 systems from the US: what is known about them
articles.body:
Ukraine will receive new missiles for S-300 systems from the US: what is known about them
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine may receive the S-300 Clone and GAM-67 in a US air defense package worth up to $2.68 billion. The missiles are compatible with some Soviet-era air defense systems.
Ukraine is to receive new S-300 Clone and GAM-67 surface-to-air missiles as part of a U.S.-approved air defense components package worth up to $2.68 billion. These are new developments, some of which will be compatible with Soviet-made systems already in service with the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
The package will also include Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket systems, Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5 launchers, RPS 202 radars for detecting drones, and other equipment.
The procurement is planned to be financed through contributions from European partners and unused funds from the U.S. Foreign Military Financing program for Ukraine.
What is known about the new missiles
According to Defense Express, despite its name, the S-300 Clone is not a copy of the Soviet 5V55 missile. It is a new missile for S-300 systems, featuring enhanced capabilities and a more modern target-guidance principle.
The GAM-67 is also a new development. It is being created for medium-range air defense systems, including existing Soviet-designed systems and advanced surface-to-air missile systems.
Defense Express notes that development of both missiles has been underway for some time, while funding for the projects has intensified recently. One potential advantage of these missiles could be their versatility and ability to be used with various surface-to-air systems.
In the future, such solutions could also allow countries that still operate Soviet- or Russian-made surface-to-air missile systems to obtain new missiles without depending on supplies from Russia.

articles.title: Top NATO commander joins briefing on review of US defence engagement in Europe
articles.body:
Top NATO commander joins briefing on review of US defence engagement in Europe
BRUSSELS, Sept 18 - NATO's top commander, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, took part in a virtual briefing on Friday for Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on potential approaches to a review of US troop deployments in Europe.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a review in June of America's troop deployments in Europe and threatened to withhold some US dues to NATO if "free riding" allies did not meet their defence spending commitments.
Grynkewich took part in Friday's meeting in his capacity as head of the US European Command "as Europe continues to take more and more responsibility for its defence, and as the Alliance continues to strengthen and transition to 'NATO 3.0'", a NATO spokesperson said.
A document seen by Reuters shows the review will create at least four sets of options for Hegseth, with Friday's briefing contributing to shaping the possibilities on the table.
Hegseth told defence ministers at NATO headquarters in Brussels in June that the review would last up to six months and include consultations with Congress, which has legislated a minimum number of US forces in Europe.
While he did not explicitly say the review could result in reductions of the 80,000 US troops deployed to Europe, he stressed the goal would be to prompt the continent to do more while ensuring the US military would be able to meet its global commitments.
Hegseth also slammed allies who did not support the US during the Iran war, after some denied Washington basing and overflight rights for war-related activities, and said the review would ensure these rights were assured. REUTERS

articles.title: Russian glide bomb hits apartment in Ukraine's Sumy, two dead, seven injured
articles.body:
Russian glide bomb hits apartment in Ukraine's Sumy, two dead, seven injured
Sept 18 - A Russian glide bomb hit an apartment building in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Friday, killing two people and injuring seven, leaving three of them in serious condition, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and other officials said.
Zelenskiy, writing on the Telegram messaging app, denounced the "absolutely inhuman strike". He said emergency crews had rescued four people after the attack and said others could still be trapped under rubble.
"There was a direct hit by an aerial bomb between the third and fourth floors. Four people have already been rescued from under the rubble, including a child," he wrote. "There may still be people under the rubble."
Zelenskiy posted pictures on Telegram showing the shattered facade of the building and rescue workers making their way through debris.
The head of Sumy city council said the two dead were city employees.
Regional Governor Oleh Hryhorov said three of the seven injured were in a serious condition. Among the injured was a 13-year-old girl.
Zelenskiy said Russian forces had also hit a clinic in the central city of Pavlohrad and a logistics centre outside Kyiv, but provided no details on casualties.
An earlier Russian strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Balakliia killed two people and wounded two, Vitali Karabanov, the head of the city's military administration, said on Telegram.
Sumy, near the Russian border, has been a frequent Russian target in an area where Moscow says it wants to establish a buffer zone.
Balakliia, located in Kharkiv region, was captured by Russian forces in the early weeks of Moscow's February 2022 full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbour, but retaken by Ukrainian troops in a large counteroffensive later in the year.
The Ukrainian capital Kyiv had come under a Russian missile attack earlier in the evening, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, but there was no indication of casualties or damage.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war. REUTERS

articles.title: Secret F-35 technology ended up in Hong Kong; the US is conducting an investigation — media

Kyiv • UNN

Secret technologies from the American F-35 fighter jet were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong. The United States has launched an investigation into how aircraft parts ended up in Hong Kong. Politico reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
This summer, secret technologies from the F-35 fighter jet were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, prompting an investigation on Capitol Hill and giving rise to speculation that China may have gained access to key components of the highly classified weapons system
A shipment of F-35 parts bound for the United States for repairs was diverted while in transit across the Pacific from Australia. The Pentagon confirmed that some components had gone missing.
The parts, which an intermediary was transporting on behalf of the F-35 manufacturer, instead ended up in Hong Kong.
According to two sources, the shipment contained one of the aircraft's canopies, which covers the pilot's cockpit and incorporates stealth technology accessible only to the United States and its allies. If one of these canopies fell into an adversary's hands, they could study its details and potentially reverse-engineer this valuable technology.

The United States approved a potential sale to Saudi Arabia of 48 F-35 fighter jets worth $24.3 billion. The State Department announced on Thursday that it had approved the possible sale of the aircraft and related equipment.

articles.title: Canada seeks to join €90bn support loan for Ukraine, Brussels confirms
articles.body:
Canada's inclusion will allow Ukraine to buy weapons from Canadian defence companies and bypass the "Made in Europe" requirements. In turn, Ottawa will have to pay a proportional share of the annual interest.
Canada is seeking to join the European Union's €90 billion support loan for Ukraine, the European Commission said on Friday.
"I can confirm that Canada has expressed an interest in joining the €90 billion Ukraine support loan," a Commission spokesperson told journalists. "We are working hard with Canada, and the respective technical talks are very much ongoing."
EU leaders set up the loan to meet two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027, with the other third covered by other Western allies.
So far, Brussels has disbursed nearly €15 billion, with more instalments expected soon.
The €90 billion is raised through joint borrowing and generates about €3 billion in annual interest payments, which will be paid proportionally by 24 member states. (Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic secured an opt-out from the scheme.)
Canada's inclusion, if successful, will allow Ukraine to procure weapons and ammunition from Canadian defence companies and bypass the "Made in Europe" requirements that govern the credit line. In turn, Ottawa will have to pay a share of the €3 billion in interest rates, depending on how much its firms benefit.
The specifics of the Canadian contribution are still under negotiation.
"The more countries involved, the better. That can ensure that Ukraine can get the best and most suitable equipment for its defence needs," the Commission spokesperson said.
The United Kingdom, a major donor to Ukraine, became the first non-EU country to join the support programme in July.
The news comes as Kyiv looks to allies to plug a growing budget deficit, which is being worsened by Russia's escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.
Brussels is trying to pin down the exact scope of Ukraine's additional needs and has asked other partners to step up. Norway recently announced $9 billion for 2027.
"It's important indeed that our like-minded partners also follow suit, including Canada and the UK," the Commission spokesperson said.
"That is a subject that we usually tend to take up with them regularly."
Canada's move to join the scheme is seen as part of a fast-moving impetus to expand and deepen ties between Ottawa and Brussels. This week, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member".

articles.title: Putin Claims Readiness to Restore Relations With Europe
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Moscow is prepared to resume cooperation and restore diplomatic relations with its European neighbors, asserting that Russia harbors no hostile intentions toward the European continent, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Friday, Sept. 18.
Speaking during a meeting of Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission, the Russian leader insisted that the Kremlin remains open to re-establishing bilateral dialogue despite years of acute geopolitical confrontation since Moscow launched its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are ready to cooperate and restore relations with our European neighbors,” Putin stated, adding that Moscow maintains no aggressive designs against European states.
Accusations against European leadership and NATO expansion
Despite professing a desire for normalized ties, Putin used the address to criticize Western governments, asserting that external security threats against Russia have not diminished. He accused NATO of systematically expanding its global footprint and seeking to project influence into regions far beyond the North Atlantic.
Putin also directed criticism at European heads of state, alleging that several leaders have engaged in irresponsible rhetoric by openly discussing preparations for potential armed conflict with Russia.
The Russian leader claimed that such military warnings represent deliberate political maneuvers by European officials to conceal mounting domestic economic and social crises, distract public attention from declining living standards, and recover lost electoral support.
South Korea Signs Pact With EU on Satellite Network
He asserted that European electorates had demonstrated through recent democratic elections that they oppose any direct conflict with Moscow.
European warnings of diversionary escalation
Putin’s diplomatic overtures contrast sharply with assessments delivered by European leaders, who warn that the Kremlin is actively stoking regional crises to divert scrutiny from mounting battlefield difficulties in Ukraine.
Speaking in Oslo alongside Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Thursday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni cautioned European allies to scrutinize Moscow’s underlying motivations before reacting to an intensifying wave of Russian provocations along NATO’s periphery.
Meloni argued that the recent surge in hostile activity stems directly from Russia’s inability to achieve its strategic objectives in Ukraine, noting that the invasion has failed to deliver the rapid victory promised by the Kremlin.
She warned that Putin seeks an escalation with Europe precisely to distract domestic audiences from the reality of the war, urging European nations to avoid disproportionate responses that could play directly into Moscow’s strategic calculations.

North Korea rejected the IAEA resolution and said it would not give up its nuclear status

North Korea rejected the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution concerning its nuclear program and stated that it has no intention of giving up its status as a nuclear-weapon state. Kim Yo Jong called the IAEA resolution "absurd and ineffective" and emphasized that it would not affect Pyongyang's position regarding its own nuclear arsenal.

Kim Yo Jong stated that it was fundamentally important for North Korea to maintain confidence in its own nuclear forces, accusing "hostile forces" of creating a nuclear threat to the country.
The most important issue for national security is to ensure that confidence in North Korea's nuclear forces, which are constantly exposed to a nuclear threat from hostile forces, is under no circumstances called into question
Thus, Pyongyang made it clear that the international nuclear regulator's resolution would not change its position on maintaining its nuclear arsenal.
